sections.title: Sources for Early Indian History
context: HIST 100 – HISTORY OF INDIA UP TO MAURYAN PERIOD

blocks.text: Early Indian history is reconstructed from archaeological remains, inscriptions, coins, literary traditions and material objects. Archaeology is especially important for periods before extensive written records.

Sources are divided into archaeological and literary. Archaeological sources include excavated sites (Harappa, Mohenjo-daro, Taxila), monuments (stupas, pillars, caves), inscriptions on stone and copper plates, coins (punch-marked coins, Indo-Greek, Kushana and Gupta coins) and artefacts such as pottery, tools, seals and ornaments. Epigraphy is the study of inscriptions and numismatics the study of coins. Ashoka's edicts in the Brahmi script, deciphered by James Prinsep in 1837, are among the most important early inscriptions.

Literary sources include religious texts (the Vedas, Upanishads, epics, Puranas, Buddhist Tripitaka and Jatakas, Jain Agamas), secular works (Panini's Ashtadhyayi, Kautilya's Arthashastra, Sangam poems, Kalidasa's plays) and foreign accounts (Herodotus, Megasthenes' Indica as quoted by later Greek writers, Fa-Hien, Hiuen Tsang). Historians must use these critically, because religious texts were not written as history and dates are often uncertain.

sections.title: Indus Valley Civilization
context: HIST 100 – HISTORY OF INDIA UP TO MAURYAN PERIOD

blocks.text: The Indus or Harappan civilization was an important urban civilization of the north-western subcontinent. It is known for planned settlements, craft production, trade, material culture and an organised urban life.

The civilisation flourished in its mature phase from about 2600 to 1900 BCE, across present-day Pakistan, north-western India and parts of Afghanistan - a larger area than ancient Egypt or Mesopotamia. Harappa was excavated by Daya Ram Sahni in 1921 and Mohenjo-daro by R. D. Banerji in 1922, under the Archaeological Survey of India directed by John Marshall. Other major sites include Kalibangan (Rajasthan), Lothal and Dholavira (Gujarat), Rakhigarhi (Haryana), Banawali and Chanhudaro.

Key features: planned cities divided into a raised citadel and a lower town; streets in a grid pattern; standardised baked bricks in the ratio 1:2:4; covered drains; the Great Bath at Mohenjo-daro; granaries or large warehouses; seals with animal motifs and a pictographic script of about 400 signs that remains undeciphered.

sections.title: Economy and Trade of the Indus Civilization
context: HIST 100 – HISTORY OF INDIA UP TO MAURYAN PERIOD

blocks.text: Agriculture, animal husbandry, crafts and trade formed the economic base. Standardised weights, seals and craft objects indicate organised exchange and commercial activity.

Farmers grew wheat, barley, peas, sesame, mustard and cotton (the Harappans were among the earliest cotton growers - the Greeks later called cotton 'sindon'), and rice at some sites such as Lothal and Rangpur. A ploughed field was found at Kalibangan. They domesticated cattle, sheep, goats, buffalo and pigs. Craft industries included bead-making (carnelian), shell-working, metallurgy in copper and bronze, pottery and seal-making.

Trade used standardised weights of chert, mostly cubical, in a binary and decimal system (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32...). Seals were probably used to mark goods. Lothal had a structure interpreted as a dockyard. Mesopotamian texts mention trade with 'Meluhha', usually identified with the Indus region, and Harappan seals and beads have been found in Mesopotamia and the Persian Gulf (Dilmun, modern Bahrain).

sections.title: Settlement and Material Culture
context: HIST 100 – HISTORY OF INDIA UP TO MAURYAN PERIOD

blocks.text: Harappan settlements ranged from large urban centres to smaller settlements. Brick construction, drainage, pottery, seals, ornaments and specialised crafts are important features of its material culture.

Settlements show a hierarchy: large cities such as Mohenjo-daro, Harappa, Ganweriwala, Rakhigarhi and Dholavira; smaller towns; and many villages. Uniformity across a vast area - in bricks, weights, seals, script and pottery styles - suggests common standards. Houses were built around courtyards, many with private wells and bathrooms connected to street drains. Dholavira had large water reservoirs and a three-part city plan.

Material culture includes red pottery painted in black, terracotta figurines (including the so-called mother goddess), toys (carts, animals), the bronze 'Dancing Girl' and the stone 'Priest-King' from Mohenjo-daro, seals showing a unicorn-like animal and the 'Pashupati' seal of a seated figure surrounded by animals, and ornaments of gold, silver, faience and semi-precious stones. Burials were usually extended inhumations with pottery and ornaments.

sections.title: Decline of the Indus Civilization
context: HIST 100 – HISTORY OF INDIA UP TO MAURYAN PERIOD

blocks.text: The urban Harappan system declined gradually rather than through one universally accepted cause. Historical study considers environmental change, settlement shifts and changes in economic networks among the explanations.

From about 1900 BCE, the large cities were gradually abandoned; town planning, writing, seals and standard weights disappeared, and people shifted to smaller rural settlements, especially eastward into Haryana and the Ganga-Yamuna doab and southward into Gujarat. This is called the Late Harappan phase, not a sudden collapse.

Explanations: (1) climate change and weakening monsoons; (2) changes in river courses, especially the drying of the Ghaggar-Hakra (often identified with the Saraswati) and floods on the Indus; (3) decline of trade with Mesopotamia; (4) ecological stress from deforestation and overuse of land; and (5) the older theory of an 'Aryan invasion', proposed by Mortimer Wheeler on the basis of skeletons at Mohenjo-daro, which is now rejected because the skeletons are from different periods and there is no evidence of a massacre.

sections.title: Debate on Aryans in India
context: HIST 100 – HISTORY OF INDIA UP TO MAURYAN PERIOD

blocks.text: The Aryan question concerns the origins and movement of Indo-Aryan-speaking peoples and the interpretation of linguistic, archaeological and textual evidence. The syllabus treats it as a historical debate rather than a simple settled story.

The word 'Aryan' (arya, meaning noble) appears in the Rigveda as a self-description of the people who composed it, not as a racial term. Comparative philology - starting with William Jones in 1786 - showed that Sanskrit is related to Greek, Latin, Persian and other Indo-European languages. The widely accepted view among historians is that Indo-Aryan speakers migrated into the subcontinent from Central Asia in several waves from around 2000-1500 BCE, bringing their language, horses and spoked-wheel chariots; this is a migration model, not a single violent invasion.

An alternative 'indigenous Aryan' or 'Out of India' view claims that the Vedic people originated in India and identifies them with the Harappans. Most scholars reject this because the Harappan culture lacks evidence of the horse and chariot central to Rigvedic life, and because of linguistic and recent genetic evidence (ancient DNA studies of 2018-2019 show a Steppe-related ancestry entering South Asia in the second millennium BCE). The debate also has a modern political dimension, so students should weigh the evidence critically.

sections.title: Vedic Society
context: HIST 100 – HISTORY OF INDIA UP TO MAURYAN PERIOD

blocks.text: Vedic society developed through family and kinship groups and gradually became more differentiated. Social divisions became more structured during the Later Vedic period.

In the Early Vedic or Rigvedic period (c. 1500-1000 BCE), society was organised in tribes (jana) and clans (vish); the family (kula or griha) was patriarchal. Social divisions were relatively fluid; the varna idea appears mainly in the late Purusha Sukta hymn (Book X), which describes the four varnas emerging from the body of the cosmic man. Women attended assemblies, and some composed hymns (Apala, Ghosha, Lopamudra); there was no evidence of child marriage.

In the Later Vedic period (c. 1000-600 BCE), the four varnas - Brahmana, Kshatriya, Vaishya, Shudra - became more rigid, with Shudras placed at the bottom. The gotra system and the four ashramas (brahmacharya, grihastha, vanaprastha, sannyasa) appeared. Women's status declined: they were excluded from assemblies and some rituals, although learned women like Gargi and Maitreyi appear in the Upanishads.

sections.title: Vedic Economy
context: HIST 100 – HISTORY OF INDIA UP TO MAURYAN PERIOD

blocks.text: The Early Vedic economy gave importance to pastoral activity, while agriculture and settled life became increasingly significant over time.

Rigvedic people were mainly semi-nomadic pastoralists. Cattle were the main form of wealth; the word for war was gavishti (search for cows), and a rich man was gomat. They also knew barley (yava) and some cultivation, and crafts such as carpentry, chariot-making, metalworking in copper and bronze (ayas) and weaving. There were no cities, coins or regular taxes; the tribal chief received voluntary offerings called bali.

In the Later Vedic period people moved eastward into the Ganga plain, where iron technology (from about 1000 BCE; called krishna ayas or shyama ayas) helped clear forests and cultivate land. Agriculture became the main occupation, with rice (vrihi), wheat and other crops. Painted Grey Ware pottery is associated with Later Vedic settlements. Bali became a compulsory tax, and crafts and specialised occupations expanded.

sections.title: Vedic Polity
context: HIST 100 – HISTORY OF INDIA UP TO MAURYAN PERIOD

blocks.text: Early political organisation was connected with tribal and kinship structures. Later Vedic developments show stronger territorial political institutions and growing authority of rulers.

The Rigvedic chief (rajan) was a tribal leader whose main duty was to protect the tribe and its cattle in war. His power was limited by tribal assemblies: the sabha (council of elders), samiti (general assembly of the tribe), vidatha (the oldest assembly, with religious and military functions) and gana. Officials included the purohita (priest), senani (army leader) and gramani (village headman). The famous 'Battle of Ten Kings' (dasarajna), in which Sudas of the Bharata tribe defeated a coalition on the river Parushni (Ravi), shows inter-tribal conflict.

In the Later Vedic period, tribes merged into larger units and territorial states emerged; the word rashtra appears. The king's power increased, supported by elaborate rituals such as the rajasuya (consecration), ashvamedha (horse sacrifice) and vajapeya (chariot race). Assemblies declined in importance, and a group of officials called the ratnins helped the king.

sections.title: Vedic Religion
context: HIST 100 – HISTORY OF INDIA UP TO MAURYAN PERIOD

blocks.text: Vedic religion centred on deities, hymns and sacrificial rituals. Later developments encouraged deeper philosophical reflection.

Rigvedic religion worshipped natural forces personified as gods. Indra, god of thunder and war, has about 250 hymns; Agni, god of fire and messenger between humans and gods, about 200; Varuna upheld rita, the cosmic and moral order; Soma was a sacred plant drink and deity; others include Surya, Ushas (dawn), Vayu and the Maruts. Worship was through hymns and simple sacrifices (yajna) to gain cattle, children, health and victory; there were no temples or idols.

In the Later Vedic period, Prajapati (the creator), Vishnu and Rudra became prominent while Indra and Agni declined. Sacrifices became elaborate, expensive and controlled by priests, increasing Brahmana power. The Brahmanas (ritual texts) and Aranyakas (forest texts) were composed. Reaction against ritualism led to the philosophical speculations of the Upanishads.

sections.title: Upanishads
context: HIST 100 – HISTORY OF INDIA UP TO MAURYAN PERIOD

blocks.text: The Upanishads developed philosophical discussions about existence, knowledge, the self and ultimate reality. They emerged from changes in the material and ideological world of the Later Vedic period.

The Upanishads (from upa-ni-shad, 'sitting down near' a teacher) are the concluding part of the Vedas, called Vedanta. About 108 are known, of which some thirteen are principal, including the Brihadaranyaka, Chandogya, Katha, Isha, Mundaka and Taittiriya. They were composed mainly between about 800 and 500 BCE.

Central ideas: Brahman is the ultimate reality behind the universe; Atman is the individual self; and they are identical ('Tat tvam asi' - That thou art). Other concepts include karma (actions determine future births), samsara (cycle of rebirth) and moksha (liberation through knowledge, jnana, rather than ritual). Kshatriya thinkers such as Janaka of Videha participated in debates. The Mundaka Upanishad gives India's national motto, 'Satyameva Jayate'.

sections.title: Janapadas and Mahajanapadas
context: HIST 100 – HISTORY OF INDIA UP TO MAURYAN PERIOD

blocks.text: Territorial states known as Janapadas developed and some expanded into larger Mahajanapadas. Their rise marked an important stage in state formation in northern India.

Janapada means the place where a jana (tribe) settled. By the sixth century BCE, these had grown into sixteen Mahajanapadas, listed in the Buddhist Anguttara Nikaya and the Jain Bhagavati Sutra: Anga, Magadha, Kashi, Kosala, Vajji, Malla, Chedi, Vatsa, Kuru, Panchala, Matsya, Shurasena, Ashmaka, Avanti, Gandhara and Kamboja.

Most were monarchies, but some, such as the Vajji confederacy (with the Lichchhavis at Vaishali) and the Mallas, were ganas or sanghas - oligarchies or republics governed by assemblies of clan heads. Their rise was linked with iron tools, agricultural surplus, the growth of towns (the 'second urbanisation'), the use of punch-marked coins and regular taxation. Over time, Magadha, Kosala, Vatsa and Avanti became the four most powerful, and Magadha finally absorbed the others.

sections.title: Rise of Magadha
context: HIST 100 – HISTORY OF INDIA UP TO MAURYAN PERIOD

blocks.text: Magadha became a dominant political power because of a combination of strategic location, resources, military strength and capable rulers.

Rulers: the Haryanka dynasty - Bimbisara (c. 544-492 BCE), who expanded through conquest (Anga) and marriage alliances with Kosala, Lichchhavi and Madra families; his son Ajatashatru, who defeated Kosala and the Vajji confederacy using new weapons (catapult, mahashilakantaka, and a chariot with maces, rathamusala) and fortified Pataliputra; Udayin, who made Pataliputra the capital. The Shishunagas then destroyed Avanti, and the Nandas under Mahapadma Nanda built a large empire with a huge army and treasury.

Reasons for Magadha's rise: fertile alluvial soil of the middle Ganga plain; rich iron deposits nearby in present-day Jharkhand; forests supplying elephants for the army; strategic capitals - Rajagriha, protected by five hills, and Pataliputra at the confluence of the Ganga, Son and Gandak - which controlled river trade; a mixed, less orthodox society; and ambitious, capable rulers.

sections.title: Buddhism
context: HIST 100 – HISTORY OF INDIA UP TO MAURYAN PERIOD

blocks.text: Buddhism arose as a heterodox religious tradition associated with Gautama Buddha. It emphasised the problem of suffering and a path toward liberation.

Siddhartha Gautama (c. 563-483 BCE, or later by some estimates) was born at Lumbini (in present-day Nepal) in the Shakya clan of Kapilavastu. After seeing an old man, a sick man, a corpse and an ascetic, he left home at 29 (the Great Renunciation), attained enlightenment at Bodh Gaya under the pipal tree at 35, gave his first sermon at Sarnath (Dharmachakra Pravartana) and died at Kushinagar (Mahaparinirvana).

Teachings: the Four Noble Truths - life is full of suffering (dukkha), suffering has a cause (desire, tanha), it can be ended (nirvana), and there is a path to end it - the Eightfold Path (right view, intention, speech, action, livelihood, effort, mindfulness, concentration). He preached the Middle Way between luxury and severe asceticism, rejected Vedic sacrifices and caste privilege and taught in Pali, the language of the people. The Sangha (monastic order), the Tripitaka (Vinaya, Sutta, Abhidhamma) and royal patrons like Bimbisara and later Ashoka spread Buddhism.

sections.title: Jainism
context: HIST 100 – HISTORY OF INDIA UP TO MAURYAN PERIOD

blocks.text: Jainism, strongly associated with Mahavira, emphasised non-violence, discipline and liberation from the cycle of rebirth.

Jainism has twenty-four tirthankaras; Rishabhadeva is regarded as the first, Parshvanatha the twenty-third and Vardhamana Mahavira (c. 540-468 BCE) the twenty-fourth. Mahavira was born at Kundagrama near Vaishali, became an ascetic at 30, attained kevala jnana (supreme knowledge) after twelve years and died at Pavapuri. He was called Jina (conqueror), from which 'Jain' comes.

Teachings: the three jewels (triratna) - right faith, right knowledge and right conduct; five vows - ahimsa (non-violence), satya (truth), asteya (non-stealing), aparigraha (non-possession) and brahmacharya (celibacy, added by Mahavira); the belief that all things, even stones and water, have souls (jiva); and severe asceticism to remove karma. Later the religion split into the Digambaras (sky-clad) and Shvetambaras (white-clad). Jainism appealed especially to traders, and Chandragupta Maurya is said to have become a Jain.

sections.title: Ajivikas
context: HIST 100 – HISTORY OF INDIA UP TO MAURYAN PERIOD

blocks.text: The Ajivikas were one of the heterodox sects that emerged in ancient India. They formed part of the wider religious and philosophical ferment of the period.

The Ajivika sect was founded or led by Makkhali Gosala, who was for a time a companion of Mahavira before they quarrelled. Their central doctrine was niyati (fate or destiny): every event, including a person's rebirths and final liberation, is predetermined, and human effort cannot change it. They practised severe asceticism and nakedness.

The Ajivikas are known mainly from hostile Buddhist and Jain accounts, since their own texts are lost. They enjoyed royal patronage: Ashoka and his grandson Dasharatha donated the Barabar and Nagarjuni caves near Gaya to them, which are among the earliest rock-cut caves in India. The sect survived in South India until about the fourteenth century.

sections.title: Macedonian Invasion
context: HIST 100 – HISTORY OF INDIA UP TO MAURYAN PERIOD

blocks.text: Alexander of Macedon's invasion brought north-western India into direct military contact with the Macedonian world. Its long-term significance is considered in relation to political and cultural contacts.

Alexander, king of Macedon, defeated the Persian Empire and crossed into India in 326 BCE. He received the submission of Ambhi, ruler of Taxila, and defeated Porus (Puru) in the Battle of the Hydaspes (Jhelum). Impressed by Porus' courage, he restored his kingdom. When his army reached the river Beas (Hyphasis), the soldiers refused to go further, partly because of reports of the powerful Nanda army. Alexander returned and died at Babylon in 323 BCE.

Effects: the invasion lasted only about nineteen months, but it opened routes between India and the West, led to Greek settlements in the north-west, created a political vacuum that helped Chandragupta Maurya unite northern India, and produced Greek accounts of India. Later Greek influence appears in Gandhara art and in coinage and astronomy, mainly through the Indo-Greeks.

sections.title: Rise of the Mauryan Empire
context: HIST 100 – HISTORY OF INDIA UP TO MAURYAN PERIOD

blocks.text: The Mauryan Empire emerged under Chandragupta Maurya and became one of the largest early empires of the subcontinent.

Chandragupta Maurya (c. 321-297 BCE), helped by his adviser Chanakya (Kautilya, Vishnugupta), overthrew Dhana Nanda and captured Pataliputra. He then expelled Greek garrisons from the north-west and in about 305 BCE defeated Seleucus Nicator, Alexander's general, gaining Arachosia, Gedrosia, Paropamisadae and part of Aria (in present-day Afghanistan and Baluchistan) in return for 500 elephants; a marriage alliance was also concluded. Seleucus sent Megasthenes as ambassador to the Mauryan court.

His son Bindusara (c. 297-273 BCE), called Amitraghata ('slayer of enemies') by the Greeks, extended the empire into the Deccan. Ashoka (c. 268-232 BCE) conquered Kalinga in about 261 BCE. At its height the empire extended from Afghanistan to Bengal and from the Himalayas to Karnataka, excluding the far south. Sources include the Arthashastra, Megasthenes' Indica, Ashoka's edicts and Vishakhadatta's later drama Mudrarakshasa.

sections.title: Mauryan Administration
context: HIST 100 – HISTORY OF INDIA UP TO MAURYAN PERIOD

blocks.text: Mauryan rule involved a monarchy supported by officials and administrative arrangements across a large territory. The nature and degree of central control remain important subjects of historical study.

The king was at the centre, assisted by a council of ministers (mantriparishad). The Arthashastra describes a large bureaucracy: the samaharta (chief revenue collector), sannidhata (treasurer) and many adhyakshas (superintendents) of departments such as trade, agriculture, mines, weights and measures, forests, ships and liquor. A system of spies (gudhapurushas) kept watch on officials and people. Megasthenes describes six committees of five members each that administered Pataliputra.

The empire was divided into provinces governed by princes (kumaras) from Taxila, Ujjain, Tosali and Suvarnagiri, with Magadha under direct rule; below came districts and villages. Ashoka appointed rajukas (land and judicial officers) and dhamma-mahamattas. The army was large and organised by a war office. Recent historians (Romila Thapar) argue that control was strongest in the core region and weaker in the outlying areas.

sections.title: Mauryan Economy
context: HIST 100 – HISTORY OF INDIA UP TO MAURYAN PERIOD

blocks.text: Agriculture, taxation, crafts and trade supported the Mauryan state. The empire's size connected several economic regions.

Agriculture was the main source of revenue. The state collected bhaga, a share of the produce usually one-sixth (sometimes more), plus other taxes like bali and pindakara. The state owned crown lands (sita) worked by slaves and labourers, and helped irrigation - the Sudarshana lake at Girnar in Saurashtra was built under Chandragupta's governor Pushyagupta. Forests, mines, salt and the manufacture of weapons were state monopolies.

Crafts and trade flourished; guilds (shrenis) were important. Silver punch-marked coins (pana) were widely used. Roads connected the empire, including the Uttarapatha from Taxila to Pataliputra. Trade linked India with Central Asia, West Asia and Sri Lanka. Northern Black Polished Ware (NBPW), a glossy pottery, is a hallmark of the period. Megasthenes' account of seven castes in India reflects the occupational divisions he observed.

sections.title: Mauryan Art and Architecture
context: HIST 100 – HISTORY OF INDIA UP TO MAURYAN PERIOD

blocks.text: Mauryan cultural remains include pillars, polished stone work, stupas and other monuments associated particularly with imperial patronage.

Mauryan art can be divided into court art and popular art. Court art includes the monolithic sandstone pillars with a mirror-like polish, quarried at Chunar, which carry Ashoka's edicts and are topped by animal capitals - the most famous being the Lion Capital of Sarnath, with four lions and the Dharmachakra, adopted as India's national emblem. Other capitals include the bull at Rampurva and lion at Lauriya Nandangarh. Remains of a pillared hall at Kumrahar (Pataliputra) and wooden palisades described by Megasthenes show palace architecture.

Ashoka is credited with building many stupas, including the original brick core of the Sanchi stupa. The Barabar caves (Lomas Rishi cave with a carved doorway imitating wood) are early rock-cut architecture. Popular art includes the Didarganj Yakshi (a polished stone figure of a woman holding a chauri), yaksha figures and terracotta.

sections.title: Ashoka's Dhamma
context: HIST 100 – HISTORY OF INDIA UP TO MAURYAN PERIOD

blocks.text: Ashoka's Dhamma was a policy of ethical conduct communicated through inscriptions. It stressed values such as restraint, respect, humane behaviour and concern for social harmony.

Ashoka's Dhamma (Prakrit for Sanskrit dharma) was not identical with Buddhism, although influenced by it. After the Kalinga war (described in Major Rock Edict XIII), in which 100,000 were killed and 150,000 deported, Ashoka felt remorse and replaced conquest by war (bherighosha) with conquest by dhamma (dhammaghosha).

Principles: obedience to parents and elders; respect for teachers, Brahmanas and shramanas; kindness to slaves and servants; non-violence towards animals (restrictions on sacrifice and hunting); tolerance of all sects (Rock Edict XII asks people to honour other sects); moderation in spending; and avoidance of meaningless rituals. To spread it, he appointed dhamma-mahamattas, toured as dhammayatras, set up hospitals for humans and animals, planted trees and dug wells, and sent missions abroad, including his son Mahendra and daughter Sanghamitra to Sri Lanka. The edicts were written mostly in Prakrit in the Brahmi script, and in Kharoshthi, Greek and Aramaic in the north-west.

sections.title: Decline of the Mauryan Empire
context: HIST 100 – HISTORY OF INDIA UP TO MAURYAN PERIOD

blocks.text: The Mauryan Empire weakened after Ashoka. Historians examine succession problems, regional forces, administrative pressures and other factors rather than relying on one single cause.

After Ashoka's death in about 232 BCE, the empire was divided and the later Mauryas were weak. In about 185 BCE the last Maurya, Brihadratha, was killed by his commander Pushyamitra Shunga, who founded the Shunga dynasty.

Explanations: (1) H. P. Shastri's Brahmanical reaction theory - Ashoka's pro-Buddhist policies angered Brahmanas, shown by a Brahmana general killing the last Maurya; (2) the pacifist theory - Ashoka's emphasis on non-violence weakened the army (criticised, since he retained the army); (3) weak successors and division of the empire; (4) financial crisis from the huge army and bureaucracy; (5) oppressive provincial rule, leading to revolts in places like Taxila; (6) Greek invasions in the north-west; and (7) Romila Thapar's view that the highly centralised administration depended on the king personally and did not create loyalty to the state.

sections.title: Indus Valley Civilization
context: HIST 100 – HISTORY OF INDIA UP TO MAURYAN PERIOD

blocks.text:
The Indus Valley Civilization represents one of the earliest major urban developments in South Asian history. Historical understanding of it depends largely on archaeological evidence. Its settlements show planned construction, drainage, craft specialisation and a developed material culture.

Agriculture and animal husbandry supported the economy, while seals, standardised weights and specialised products indicate organised trade and commerce. The civilization also had distinctive religious and social practices, although the undeciphered script limits certainty about its political organisation and beliefs.

Its decline was a gradual historical process. Rather than explaining it through a single event, historians examine environmental changes, shifting settlements and changes in economic and social networks.

Stages: Early Harappan (c. 3300-2600 BCE, e.g. Kot Diji, Amri, early Kalibangan), Mature Harappan (c. 2600-1900 BCE) and Late Harappan (c. 1900-1300 BCE). The civilisation covered about 1.5 million square kilometres, from Shortughai in Afghanistan and Manda in Jammu in the north to Daimabad in Maharashtra in the south, and from Sutkagendor near the Iran border to Alamgirpur in western Uttar Pradesh.

Town planning was its most striking feature. Cities had a citadel (on a raised platform, containing large public buildings such as the Great Bath and the 'granary' at Mohenjo-daro) and a lower town of houses. Roads crossed at right angles; drains were covered and had inspection holes; houses had wells, bathrooms and courtyards, but doors and windows did not face the main streets. Dholavira was divided into three parts and had a sophisticated water management system.

Religion: terracotta female figurines suggest worship of a mother goddess; the Pashupati seal suggests a proto-Shiva figure; fire altars at Kalibangan and Lothal suggest fire rituals; there was reverence for trees (pipal), animals (the humped bull) and possibly the swastika symbol. Political organisation is uncertain - the uniformity suggests some central authority, perhaps a priestly or merchant elite, but no palaces or royal tombs have been found. Some scholars suggest several city-states.

Decline: the most accepted explanation combines climatic change, the drying up of the Ghaggar-Hakra river, flooding, collapse of long-distance trade and ecological degradation. The Aryan invasion theory has been rejected. The decline was a process of de-urbanisation, and many elements - agricultural practices, crafts and religious symbols - continued into later Indian culture.

sections.title: Vedic Period
context: HIST 100 – HISTORY OF INDIA UP TO MAURYAN PERIOD

blocks.text:
The Vedic period is studied through literary traditions together with archaeological and linguistic evidence. The syllabus specifically includes the debate on Aryans in India, reminding students that questions of origin and migration require critical examination of different kinds of evidence.

Vedic society, economy, polity and religion changed over time. Pastoralism was important in the earlier phase, while agriculture and territorial settlement became more significant later. Political institutions also moved toward stronger territorial organisation.

Religious life centred on Vedic deities and sacrifice, while the later intellectual environment contributed to the philosophical discussions found in the Upanishads.

Sources: the four Vedas - Rigveda (hymns), Samaveda (melodies), Yajurveda (sacrificial formulas) and Atharvaveda (charms and spells) - followed by the Brahmanas, Aranyakas and Upanishads. The Rigveda is the earliest, composed around 1500-1000 BCE in ten books (mandalas); the others belong to the Later Vedic period. The geography of the Rigveda is the 'land of seven rivers' (Sapta Sindhu) in Punjab and Afghanistan; Later Vedic texts show a shift eastward to the Ganga-Yamuna doab and beyond. Archaeologically, the Later Vedic phase is linked with Painted Grey Ware.

The Aryan debate: the linguistic relationship between Sanskrit and other Indo-European languages, the similarity between the Rigveda and the Iranian Avesta, and the central role of horses and chariots support the view that Indo-Aryan speakers migrated into India gradually from the north-west around the second millennium BCE. Historians such as R. S. Sharma and Romila Thapar describe this as migrations and interactions with local people rather than a single invasion. Some argue for an indigenous origin, but this has little archaeological or linguistic support.

Changes from Early to Later Vedic: (1) economy moved from pastoralism to settled agriculture using iron; (2) the tribal chief became a territorial king with a more elaborate administration, while popular assemblies declined; (3) varna became rigid and hereditary, with Brahmanas and Kshatriyas dominant and Shudras subordinated, and women's status declined; (4) religion moved from nature worship and simple sacrifices to elaborate priestly rituals and new gods like Prajapati, Vishnu and Rudra; (5) the Upanishads reacted against ritualism and emphasised knowledge of Brahman and Atman, karma, samsara and moksha.

sections.title: Post-Vedic Political and Religious Developments
context: HIST 100 – HISTORY OF INDIA UP TO MAURYAN PERIOD

blocks.text:
The post-Vedic period witnessed the rise of territorial states known as Janapadas and Mahajanapadas. Among them, Magadha achieved political ascendancy because of favourable resources, strategic position, military power and political leadership.

The period also witnessed important heterodox traditions. Buddhism, Jainism and the Ajivikas challenged or offered alternatives to established religious practices. Buddhism and Jainism in particular became major traditions with lasting influence.

Alexander's Macedonian invasion affected north-western India and created another point of contact between India and the wider Hellenistic world.

The sixth century BCE is called a period of 'second urbanisation' (after the Harappan). Iron tools, wet rice cultivation, agricultural surplus, trade, coins (punch-marked) and the growth of towns such as Rajagriha, Shravasti, Kaushambi, Varanasi, Ujjain and Vaishali formed the material background. The sixteen Mahajanapadas included both monarchies and gana-sanghas (republics). Magadha rose through its natural resources, strategic capitals, use of elephants and capable rulers (Bimbisara, Ajatashatru, Shishunaga, Mahapadma Nanda).

Rise of new religions: the period saw about 62 sects, according to Buddhist sources. Causes: reaction against the complex and costly rituals and dominance of Brahmanas; resentment of Kshatriyas against Brahmana supremacy (both the Buddha and Mahavira were Kshatriyas); the need of the new agricultural economy to protect cattle, which were killed in sacrifices; the support of traders (Vaishyas), whose wealth was not matched by social status; and the use of Prakrit and Pali, the people's languages.

Buddhism and Jainism compared: both rejected the Vedas' authority, sacrifices and caste privilege; both believed in karma and rebirth and sought liberation; both emphasised non-violence and ethics and had monastic orders. Differences: Buddhism taught the Middle Way, while Jainism stressed extreme asceticism; Jainism believed in souls in all things, while Buddhism taught anatta (no permanent self); Buddhism spread widely in Asia, while Jainism remained mainly in India. The Ajivikas taught strict fatalism (niyati).

Alexander's invasion (327-325 BCE) affected only the north-west, but it opened sea and land routes, provided dates for Indian chronology (Sandrokottos = Chandragupta) and weakened the small states of the north-west, helping the Mauryan unification of India.

sections.title: Mauryan Empire
context: HIST 100 – HISTORY OF INDIA UP TO MAURYAN PERIOD

blocks.text:
The Mauryan Empire emerged under Chandragupta Maurya and created an extensive political structure. Administration required officials, taxation and arrangements for governing different regions. Agriculture, crafts and trade supported the imperial economy.

Mauryan art and architecture include important examples of stone work, pillars and Buddhist monuments. Ashoka is especially remembered for inscriptions communicating his Dhamma, an ethical policy stressing restraint, humane conduct and social harmony.

After Ashoka, Mauryan power weakened. The decline is best understood through several political, administrative and regional factors rather than a single explanation.

Foundation and expansion: Chandragupta (with Kautilya) overthrew the Nandas, defeated Seleucus and conquered much of India; according to Jain tradition he became a Jain monk and died at Shravanabelagola in Karnataka. Bindusara extended the empire southwards. Ashoka, initially governor of Taxila and Ujjain, conquered Kalinga, after which he renounced war and followed Dhamma. He also convened the Third Buddhist Council at Pataliputra (c. 250 BCE) under Moggaliputta Tissa.

Administration: a centralised monarchy with a council of ministers and a large bureaucracy, described in the Arthashastra; provinces under princes; the city administration of Pataliputra described by Megasthenes; spies; a large standing army; and a judicial system with dharmasthiya (civil) and kantakashodhana (criminal) courts. Economy: land revenue (usually one-sixth), state control over mines, forests and some industries, crown lands, irrigation works, punch-marked coins, guilds, roads and foreign trade.

Art and Dhamma: polished Chunar sandstone pillars with animal capitals, stupas, rock-cut caves and yaksha sculptures are the main remains. Ashoka's edicts - 14 Major Rock Edicts, Minor Rock Edicts, 7 Pillar Edicts and others - spread his Dhamma of tolerance, non-violence and welfare. Decline: weak successors, financial strain, Brahmanical reaction (debated), provincial revolts, Greek invasions and over-centralisation. Pushyamitra Shunga ended the dynasty in about 185 BCE. The Mauryas created the first pan-Indian empire and left an important legacy in administration and ethics.

context: HIST 101 – HISTORY OF INDIA FROM POST-MAURYA TO GUPTA PERIOD

sections.title: Post-Mauryan Invasions
context: HIST 101 – HISTORY OF INDIA FROM POST-MAURYA TO GUPTA PERIOD

blocks.text: After the Mauryas, north-western India experienced the arrival and rule of groups such as Indo-Greeks, Shakas and Kushanas. These contacts influenced politics, trade and culture.

Indo-Greeks (Bactrian Greeks) entered the north-west in the second century BCE; the most famous ruler, Menander (Milinda), had his capital at Sakala (Sialkot) and is said to have become a Buddhist after discussions with the monk Nagasena (recorded in the Milindapanho). The Indo-Greeks issued the first Indian coins with portraits of kings and inscriptions, and gold coins. The Heliodorus pillar at Besnagar records a Greek ambassador's devotion to Vasudeva (Vishnu).

The Shakas (Scythians) came from Central Asia; the Western Kshatrapas ruled Gujarat and Malwa, and Rudradaman I's Junagadh inscription (150 CE) is the first long inscription in Sanskrit and records the repair of the Sudarshana lake. The Parthians (Pahlavas), including Gondophernes, are associated in legend with St Thomas. The Kushanas, a branch of the Yuezhi, followed. These groups became assimilated into Indian society, often as Kshatriyas.

sections.title: Satavahanas
context: HIST 101 – HISTORY OF INDIA FROM POST-MAURYA TO GUPTA PERIOD

blocks.text: The Satavahanas became an important power in the Deccan and played a major role in regional politics and economic networks.

The Satavahanas (also called Andhras) ruled the Deccan from about the first century BCE to the third century CE, with capitals at Pratishthana (Paithan) and later Amaravati. Simuka is regarded as the founder. Gautamiputra Satakarni (c. 106-130 CE) was the greatest ruler; his mother Gautami Balashri's Nasik inscription praises him for defeating the Shakas, Yavanas and Pahlavas and destroying the Kshaharata ruler Nahapana. Kings used matronymics (names derived from mothers).

They were Brahmanical rulers but patronised Buddhism; they began the practice of granting land, especially to Brahmanas and Buddhist monks, with tax exemptions. The Deccan economy prospered through agriculture, guilds and trade, including Indo-Roman trade through western ports such as Bharukachchha (Broach) and Sopara. Buddhist monuments such as the Karle chaitya, Nasik caves and the Amaravati stupa belong to this period. Prakrit was the official language.

sections.title: Kushanas
context: HIST 101 – HISTORY OF INDIA FROM POST-MAURYA TO GUPTA PERIOD

blocks.text: The Kushanas controlled important territories in north-western and northern India and were closely connected with long-distance trade and cultural exchange.

The Kushanas belonged to the Yuezhi tribes of Central Asia. Kujula Kadphises established their power in the north-west; Vima Kadphises issued many gold coins. Kanishka (accession usually dated to 78 CE, the start of the Shaka era used by the Indian national calendar), was the greatest ruler. His empire extended from Central Asia (Bactria) to the Ganga plain, with capitals at Purushapura (Peshawar) and Mathura.

Kanishka patronised Mahayana Buddhism and convened the Fourth Buddhist Council in Kashmir under Vasumitra. His court included Ashvaghosha (author of the Buddhacharita), Nagarjuna and the physician Charaka. The Kushanas controlled a section of the Silk Route linking China, Central Asia, India and the Roman Empire, which brought wealth and cultural exchange. They used titles such as 'devaputra' (son of god) and issued large numbers of gold coins depicting Greek, Iranian, Indian and Buddhist deities. Gandhara and Mathura art flourished under them.

sections.title: Crafts and Guilds
context: HIST 101 – HISTORY OF INDIA FROM POST-MAURYA TO GUPTA PERIOD

blocks.text: Craft production expanded in many centres. Guilds organised artisans and merchants and became important institutions in urban and commercial life.

Texts such as the Milindapanho and the Mahavastu mention dozens of crafts - weavers, goldsmiths, blacksmiths, ivory workers, potters, perfumers, carpenters and others. Mathura, Ujjain, Taxila, Varanasi and Arikamedu were important craft centres. Textiles (especially fine cotton and muslin), beads and iron goods were notable.

Guilds (shreni) were associations of artisans or merchants of the same occupation, headed by a jyeshthaka or shreshthin. They had their own rules (shrenidharma) recognised by the state, settled disputes, regulated quality and prices, and acted as banks, accepting deposits and paying interest; inscriptions at Nasik record deposits with weavers' guilds whose interest was used for donations. Guilds also donated to Buddhist monasteries and had their own seals and banners.

sections.title: Indo-Roman Trade
context: HIST 101 – HISTORY OF INDIA FROM POST-MAURYA TO GUPTA PERIOD

blocks.text: Commercial connections linked India with the Roman world through maritime and overland routes. Indian products participated in wider exchange networks.

Indo-Roman trade flourished in the first and second centuries CE, especially after the Romans learned to use the monsoon winds for direct sailing across the Arabian Sea (credited in Greek sources to Hippalus). The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea (first century CE), written by an anonymous Greek merchant, describes ports such as Barbaricum, Barygaza (Broach), Muziris (Kerala), Poduca (Arikamedu, near Puducherry) and Kaveripattinam.

India exported pepper ('black gold'), spices, precious stones, pearls, ivory, fine textiles, indigo and animals such as peacocks; it imported wine, olive oil, glassware, metals, coral and especially gold and silver coins. Large hoards of Roman coins have been found in South India, and Arikamedu has yielded Roman amphorae and Arretine pottery. The Roman writer Pliny complained that India drained the Roman Empire of 50 million sesterces a year. Much of this trade passed through Tamil and Satavahana ports.

sections.title: Post-Mauryan Architecture and Sculpture
context: HIST 101 – HISTORY OF INDIA FROM POST-MAURYA TO GUPTA PERIOD

blocks.text: The period saw major developments in architecture and sculpture, including Buddhist monuments and important artistic traditions.

Buddhist architecture flourished. Stupas - hemispherical mounds containing relics - were enlarged and decorated with stone railings and gateways (toranas), as at Sanchi (four richly carved gateways, first century BCE-first century CE), Bharhut and Amaravati. Rock-cut chaityas (prayer halls) and viharas (monasteries) were excavated in the western Deccan, at Karle, Bhaja, Nasik, Ajanta (early caves) and Kanheri. The Udayagiri-Khandagiri caves in Odisha were made for Jain monks under Kharavela.

Sculpture developed three major schools: Gandhara (north-west), influenced by Greco-Roman art, showing the Buddha with wavy hair, a muscular body and toga-like robes, made in grey schist and stucco; Mathura, an indigenous school using spotted red sandstone, producing Buddhist, Jain and Hindu images, and the headless statue of Kanishka; and Amaravati (Andhra), using white marble with dynamic narrative reliefs. The Buddha began to be represented in human form during this period, instead of only symbols.

sections.title: Sangam Age
context: HIST 101 – HISTORY OF INDIA FROM POST-MAURYA TO GUPTA PERIOD

blocks.text: The Sangam Age is associated with early historic South India and Tamil literary traditions. Sangam literature provides evidence about society, culture, economy and political life.

Sangam (assembly) refers to three legendary assemblies of Tamil poets held at Madurai under Pandya patronage. The surviving literature, dated broadly from about the third century BCE to the third century CE, includes the Tolkappiyam (grammar), the Ettuthokai (Eight Anthologies) and Pattuppattu (Ten Idylls); the later epics Silappadikaram and Manimekalai, and the ethical Tirukkural of Tiruvalluvar, are post-Sangam. Poems are divided into akam (love, inner) and puram (war, public).

The literature describes three ruling families - the Cheras (Kerala), Cholas (Kaveri delta, port at Puhar) and Pandyas (Madurai, port at Korkai) - and chiefs called velir. It divides the land into five tinais (landscape zones) - kurinji (hills), mullai (forest pasture), marutam (wet farmland), neytal (coast) and palai (dry land) - each with its own occupations. It also describes heroic values, hero stones (natukal), bards, Indo-Roman trade and the Tamil deity Murugan.

sections.title: Gupta Empire
context: HIST 101 – HISTORY OF INDIA FROM POST-MAURYA TO GUPTA PERIOD

blocks.text: The Guptas established a major political power in northern India. Their administration combined imperial authority with significant regional and local elements.

Sri Gupta and Ghatotkacha were the early rulers. Chandragupta I (c. 319-335 CE) married the Lichchhavi princess Kumaradevi, took the title Maharajadhiraja and is linked with the start of the Gupta era in 319-320 CE. Samudragupta (c. 335-375 CE) expanded the empire through conquests described in the Allahabad Pillar inscription (Prayaga Prashasti) by his court poet Harisena; he annexed the north (aryavarta), made southern kings tributaries and then reinstated them, and is called the 'Napoleon of India' by V. A. Smith. He was also a poet and musician (shown playing the veena on coins).

Chandragupta II (c. 375-415 CE), called Vikramaditya, defeated the Shakas of western India, gaining ports on the Arabian Sea, and allied with the Vakatakas by marrying his daughter Prabhavati to Rudrasena II. The Chinese pilgrim Fa-Hien visited during his reign. Kumaragupta I founded Nalanda university, and Skandagupta resisted the Huna invasions. After about 550 CE the empire declined.

sections.title: Decentralised Administration
context: HIST 101 – HISTORY OF INDIA FROM POST-MAURYA TO GUPTA PERIOD

blocks.text: The Gupta political structure is studied for tendencies toward decentralisation, including the growing importance of local authorities and land grants.

The king had grand titles (Maharajadhiraja, Paramabhattaraka) and was compared with gods. The empire was divided into provinces (bhukti) under uparikas, districts (vishaya) under vishayapatis and villages under gramikas. Towns had councils that included the chief banker (nagarashreshthi), chief merchant (sarthavaha), chief artisan (prathama kulika) and chief scribe (prathama kayastha), showing local participation.

Decentralised features: much of the empire was ruled by feudatory or subordinate kings (samantas) who paid tribute and supplied troops, rather than by central officials; offices tended to become hereditary; officials were paid in land grants rather than cash; and land grants to Brahmanas gave them administrative and judicial rights. Historians contrast this with the centralised Mauryan administration and see it as the beginning of a more feudal structure.

sections.title: Jatidharma
context: HIST 101 – HISTORY OF INDIA FROM POST-MAURYA TO GUPTA PERIOD

blocks.text: Jatidharma refers to social duties and norms connected with caste or social groups. It forms part of the study of Gupta social structure.

By the Gupta period, society contained not only the four varnas but also many jatis (birth groups), often linked with occupation and region. The Dharmashastras of the period, such as those of Yajnavalkya, Narada and Brihaspati, describe the duties appropriate to each jati and varna - jatidharma. Mixed castes (varnasankara) were explained as products of inter-varna marriages.

Foreigners such as Greeks, Shakas and Kushanas, and tribal groups, were absorbed into the caste system as Kshatriyas or as new jatis. The Brahmana position strengthened through land grants, while the Shudras' position improved slightly in some texts as they became cultivators rather than only servants. Jatidharma made social hierarchy appear to be a sacred duty, reinforcing inequality.

sections.title: Position of Women
context: HIST 101 – HISTORY OF INDIA FROM POST-MAURYA TO GUPTA PERIOD

blocks.text: The position of women in Gupta society varied by social context. Historical study considers family norms, property, marriage and restrictions described in literary and legal traditions.

Women of the upper varnas generally had a subordinate status. Texts recommended early (even pre-puberty) marriage, emphasised obedience to husbands, and denied women independent access to Vedic study. The first evidence of sati (widow immolation) is an inscription at Eran (510 CE) recording the wife of the general Goparaja burning herself on his funeral pyre. Widow remarriage was discouraged for upper castes.

However, some women had property rights over stridhana (gifts at marriage), and Narada and others allowed remarriage in certain conditions. Royal women such as Prabhavatigupta, who ruled as regent of the Vakataka kingdom, had political power. Women appear as poets and patrons. Lower-caste and working women had different conditions, often more freedom of movement but harder labour. Thus the position varied by class, caste and region.

sections.title: Untouchability
context: HIST 101 – HISTORY OF INDIA FROM POST-MAURYA TO GUPTA PERIOD

blocks.text: The syllabus includes untouchability as an important feature in examining hierarchy and exclusion in Gupta society.

Untouchability became more pronounced in the Gupta period. The chandalas were treated as outcasts and lived outside villages and towns. Fa-Hien recorded that chandalas had to strike a piece of wood to announce their presence when entering a town so that others could avoid contact with them; they did unclean work such as handling corpses, executions and hunting.

The Dharmashastras prescribed severe restrictions on the chandalas' food, dress and residence and regarded their touch or even shadow as polluting. Their number increased as more groups were classed as impure, often tribal groups and those in occupations considered polluting. This hierarchy was justified by ideas of purity and pollution. Studying it shows how the social order excluded certain groups, a practice later challenged by reformers and abolished in Article 17 of the Indian Constitution.

sections.title: Land Grants
context: HIST 101 – HISTORY OF INDIA FROM POST-MAURYA TO GUPTA PERIOD

blocks.text: Land grants became increasingly important and transferred revenue or rights over land to religious beneficiaries and others.

The earliest known land grants were made by the Satavahanas in the first century BCE. Under the Guptas and their contemporaries (the Vakatakas), land grants became common. They were recorded on copper plates (tamrashasana). Grants to Brahmanas were called agrahara or brahmadeya; grants to temples and monasteries were devadana.

The grantee received the revenue from the land, and often rights such as exemption from tax, freedom from the entry of royal soldiers and officials, the right to collect fines and administer justice, and rights over mines and other resources. The cultivators were sometimes required to obey the new landowner. Land grants spread Brahmanical culture and agriculture into tribal and forest areas, but they also reduced the king's direct control and revenue.

sections.title: Feudalization Debate
context: HIST 101 – HISTORY OF INDIA FROM POST-MAURYA TO GUPTA PERIOD

blocks.text: The idea of feudalization is used by historians to discuss changes in land rights, political authority and agrarian relations. It is an interpretive debate, not simply a label.

Marxist historians, especially R. S. Sharma ('Indian Feudalism', 1965), and D. D. Kosambi argued that land grants created a class of landed intermediaries between the king and peasants, with political, administrative and judicial rights. Combined with the decline of trade and urban centres, the scarcity of coins, the subjection of peasants (forced labour, vishti) and the fragmentation of political power, this produced 'Indian feudalism', comparable to European feudalism, from the Gupta period onwards. Kosambi described 'feudalism from above' and 'feudalism from below'.

Critics such as Harbans Mukhia ('Was there feudalism in Indian history?', 1981), D. C. Sircar, B. D. Chattopadhyaya and Burton Stein argued that Indian peasants were not serfs, that trade and towns did not decline everywhere, and that land grants represented integration and expansion of agriculture into new areas rather than fragmentation. Chattopadhyaya proposed an 'integrative' model of state formation. The debate shows how historians interpret evidence differently.

sections.title: Gupta Agrarian Structure
context: HIST 101 – HISTORY OF INDIA FROM POST-MAURYA TO GUPTA PERIOD

blocks.text: Agriculture remained the economic base. Land grants and changing relations between rulers, intermediaries and cultivators are important to understanding the agrarian structure.

Agriculture expanded into new areas through land grants and the clearing of forests. Main crops included rice, wheat, barley, pulses, sugarcane, cotton and spices; the Amarakosha and Brihat Samhita describe various crops and agricultural knowledge. Irrigation included tanks, wells and canals; Skandagupta's Junagadh inscription records the repair of the Sudarshana lake.

The state claimed one-sixth or more of the produce as bhaga, plus other taxes such as bhoga (periodic supplies), udranga and uparikara; forced labour (vishti) was also demanded. Land ownership was debated: texts suggest the king claimed ultimate ownership but individuals had possession. The growing number of intermediaries through land grants and the obligations imposed on cultivators show changing relations between rulers, landholders and peasants.

sections.title: Gupta Trade and Coinage
context: HIST 101 – HISTORY OF INDIA FROM POST-MAURYA TO GUPTA PERIOD

blocks.text: Coins, especially gold issues, are important evidence for Gupta political and economic history. Historians also study changes in trade and currency circulation.

The Guptas issued the largest number of gold coins (called dinara, from the Roman denarius) in ancient India. They show kings in various poses - Samudragupta playing the veena or performing the ashvamedha, Chandragupta II killing a lion, Kumaragupta riding an elephant - with Sanskrit legends praising them. Silver coins were issued after the conquest of the Shakas of western India, and copper coins were few.

However, the purity of gold in later Gupta coins declined, and fewer coins were issued after Skandagupta, which some historians link to economic difficulties. Indian trade with the Roman Empire declined after the third century CE, though trade continued with Southeast Asia (Suvarnabhumi), China and the Byzantine Empire, and through ports such as Tamralipti in Bengal. The relative scarcity of low-value coins has been used in the feudalism debate to argue that local transactions were often in kind.

sections.title: Gupta Art and Architecture
context: HIST 101 – HISTORY OF INDIA FROM POST-MAURYA TO GUPTA PERIOD

blocks.text: The Gupta period witnessed important developments in temples, sculpture, painting and artistic styles.

The earliest free-standing structural Hindu temples belong to the Gupta period: the flat-roofed temple at Sanchi (Temple 17), the Dashavatara temple at Deogarh (with an early shikhara, or spire, and reliefs of Vishnu on Sheshanaga), the brick temple at Bhitargaon and the Parvati temple at Nachna. Temples had a square sanctum (garbhagriha) with a porch, beginning the Nagara style. The Udayagiri caves near Vidisha contain the great relief of Varaha (the boar incarnation of Vishnu) rescuing the earth.

Sculpture achieved a classical style with calm, spiritual expressions, as in the Sarnath Buddha (seated, preaching) and the Mathura standing Buddha. The copper Sultanganj Buddha and the iron pillar at Mehrauli (Delhi), which has not rusted for 1,600 years, show metallurgical skill. The Ajanta cave paintings (especially caves 1, 2, 16 and 17), mostly made under the Vakatakas, depict Jataka stories and the Bodhisattva Padmapani; the Bagh caves also contain paintings.

sections.title: Gupta Literature
context: HIST 101 – HISTORY OF INDIA FROM POST-MAURYA TO GUPTA PERIOD

blocks.text: Literary activity developed in Sanskrit and other traditions. Literature is an important source for understanding elite culture and intellectual life.

Sanskrit became the court language. Kalidasa, often linked with the court of Chandragupta II, wrote the plays Abhijnanashakuntalam, Malavikagnimitram and Vikramorvashiyam, and the poems Raghuvamsha, Kumarasambhava, Meghaduta and Ritusamhara. Other works include Shudraka's Mrichchhakatika (The Little Clay Cart), Vishakhadatta's Mudrarakshasa and Devichandraguptam, and the Panchatantra in its classical form. Amarasimha compiled the Amarakosha (a Sanskrit lexicon).

Science and learning advanced: Aryabhata's Aryabhatiya (499 CE) explained that the earth rotates on its axis, gave an accurate value of pi and discussed eclipses scientifically; Varahamihira wrote the Brihat Samhita and Pancha Siddhantika; and the decimal place-value system with zero developed. The Dharmashastras of Yajnavalkya, Narada and Katyayana, and philosophical works, were also written. This is why the period is sometimes called a 'classical' or 'golden' age, though that term is debated.

sections.title: Puranic Tradition
context: HIST 101 – HISTORY OF INDIA FROM POST-MAURYA TO GUPTA PERIOD

blocks.text: Puranic religious traditions became increasingly significant and contributed to developments in Hindu religious practice and sacred narratives.

The Puranas ('ancient stories') are eighteen major texts - such as the Vishnu, Vayu, Matsya, Bhagavata and Markandeya Puranas - that took their present form largely during and after the Gupta period. They cover five topics: creation, re-creation, genealogies of gods and sages, cycles of time (manvantaras) and genealogies of kings, which give useful dynastic lists. The epics Ramayana and Mahabharata, including the Bhagavad Gita, also reached their final form around this time.

Puranic Hinduism emphasised bhakti (devotion) to a personal god rather than Vedic sacrifice: Vaishnavism (worship of Vishnu and his avatars such as Rama and Krishna), Shaivism (Shiva, worshipped also as the linga) and Shaktism (the goddess). Worship (puja) in temples with images became central, along with pilgrimage, fasting and vows. The Puranas spread religious ideas in simple stories to women and Shudras as well, contributing to the synthesis of Brahmanical and local traditions.

sections.title: LONG NOTES
context: HIST 101 – HISTORY OF INDIA FROM POST-MAURYA TO GUPTA PERIOD

sections.title: Post-Mauryan Developments
context: HIST 101 – HISTORY OF INDIA FROM POST-MAURYA TO GUPTA PERIOD

blocks.text:
The period after the Mauryas saw major political and cultural changes. Invasions and migrations brought Indo-Greeks, Shakas, Kushanas and other groups into the subcontinent. The Satavahanas became important in the Deccan, while the Kushanas connected northern India with wider Central Asian networks.

Crafts, guilds and commercial centres developed, and Indo-Roman trade linked Indian producers and merchants with long-distance markets. Architecture and sculpture also flourished.

In South India, Sangam literature provides valuable evidence about society, culture, economy and political life during the early historic period.

Political situation: after the Mauryas, north India was divided. The Shungas (Pushyamitra) and Kanvas ruled Magadha; Kharavela of Kalinga (Hathigumpha inscription) was a powerful Jain king; the Satavahanas ruled the Deccan; and foreign groups - Indo-Greeks, Shakas, Parthians and Kushanas - established kingdoms in the north-west and north. Kanishka's Kushana empire connected India with Central Asia and the Silk Route. Despite political fragmentation, this was a period of economic and cultural growth.

Economy: crafts multiplied and were organised in guilds, which also functioned as banks. Towns grew, coinage in gold, silver, copper and lead increased (Kushana gold coins, Satavahana lead coins), and trade flourished along land routes (the Silk Route through the north-west) and sea routes. Indo-Roman trade brought Roman gold to India in exchange for pepper, textiles and gems, and South Indian ports such as Arikamedu and Muziris prospered.

Culture: Mahayana Buddhism developed with Bodhisattva worship and the image of the Buddha; Gandhara, Mathura and Amaravati schools of sculpture flourished; stupas at Sanchi, Bharhut and Amaravati were decorated; rock-cut caves were excavated in the Deccan. Bhakti cults of Vasudeva-Krishna grew. Sanskrit literature included Ashvaghosha's Buddhacharita, Charaka's medical text and Manu's law book. In South India, the Sangam literature describes the Chera, Chola and Pandya kingdoms, the five landscapes, heroic culture and trade.

sections.title: Gupta Administration and Society
context: HIST 101 – HISTORY OF INDIA FROM POST-MAURYA TO GUPTA PERIOD

blocks.text:
The Gupta Empire exercised authority over a large part of northern India, but its administration also contained decentralised features. Regional and local authorities gained importance, and land grants contributed to changing patterns of political and economic power.

Gupta society was hierarchical. The syllabus highlights jatidharma, women's position and untouchability as important areas of study. These topics help students understand how social status, duties and exclusion operated in the period.

Administration: the Gupta kings took high titles and were seen as divine, but they relied on samantas (feudatories) and governors who often held hereditary posts. The empire was divided into bhuktis, vishayas and villages; town councils had representatives of bankers, merchants, artisans and scribes, and village affairs were handled by headmen and elders. There was no large standing bureaucracy as under the Mauryas; officials were often paid in land. Land grants with fiscal and administrative rights reduced central control. Fa-Hien described a mild government with light taxes and rare punishments.

Society: the varna-jati system became more complex, with many new jatis formed by occupation and by the absorption of foreigners and tribes. Jatidharma - prescribed duties for each group - was promoted by the Dharmashastras. Brahmanas gained wealth and privilege through land grants. Women's status declined: early marriage, emphasis on obedience, restrictions on education and widow remarriage, and the first evidence of sati (Eran inscription, 510 CE), though they had rights over stridhana and some royal women held power. Untouchability intensified; the chandalas lived outside settlements and had to announce their presence, according to Fa-Hien.

Evaluation: older nationalist historians called the Gupta age a 'golden age'. Modern historians accept its cultural achievements but emphasise social inequality, the subordination of women and lower castes and the growth of decentralised power.

sections.title: Gupta Economy
context: HIST 101 – HISTORY OF INDIA FROM POST-MAURYA TO GUPTA PERIOD

blocks.text:
Agriculture remained central to the Gupta economy. Land grants are important because they could transfer revenue rights and contributed to changes in agrarian relations. Historians have used these developments in debates about feudalization.

Trade, coinage and currency are also important. Gupta coins provide evidence of rulers, political authority and economic life. At the same time, historians examine regional differences and changes in commercial activity.

Agrarian economy: agriculture expanded through land grants, forest clearance and irrigation. The state's share was about one-sixth of produce, plus other taxes and forced labour (vishti). Land grants to Brahmanas and religious institutions created a class of landed intermediaries who received revenue and sometimes administrative rights.

Feudalism debate: R. S. Sharma argued that land grants, the transfer of fiscal and judicial rights, payment of officials in land, decline of trade and towns and scarcity of coins led to feudalism in which peasants became dependent. Critics (Harbans Mukhia, B. D. Chattopadhyaya) argued that the Indian peasant was not a serf, that land grants helped expand agriculture and integrate new areas, and that trade continued in many regions. Students should present both sides.

Trade and coinage: the Guptas issued many high-quality gold dinaras showing kings in various poses, and silver coins after conquering western India. Foreign trade with the Roman world declined after the third century, but trade with Southeast Asia, China and Byzantium continued through ports such as Tamralipti and Bharukachchha. Guilds remained important (the Mandasor inscription records a silk weavers' guild that built a sun temple). The later debasement of coinage and fewer coins are seen as signs of economic change.

sections.title: Cultural Developments under the Guptas
context: HIST 101 – HISTORY OF INDIA FROM POST-MAURYA TO GUPTA PERIOD

blocks.text:
The Gupta period witnessed significant developments in art, architecture, painting and literature. Temples and sculpture show changing religious and artistic forms, while literary activity reflects a rich intellectual culture.

Religion also changed through the growing significance of Puranic traditions. These developments are important for understanding both continuity with earlier traditions and new cultural forms.

Architecture and art: the Gupta period marks the beginning of the Hindu temple - from flat-roofed shrines (Sanchi Temple 17, Tigawa) to temples with spires (Deogarh's Dashavatara temple, Bhitargaon). Sculpture achieved classical grace and spirituality: the Sarnath Buddha, Mathura standing Buddha, Udayagiri Varaha relief and images of Vishnu and Shiva. The Ajanta and Bagh paintings show sophisticated use of colour and line. The Mehrauli iron pillar shows advanced metallurgy.

Literature and science: Kalidasa (Shakuntalam, Meghaduta, Raghuvamsha), Shudraka, Vishakhadatta, Bharavi and the Panchatantra represent classical Sanskrit literature. Aryabhata, Varahamihira and later Brahmagupta advanced astronomy and mathematics; the decimal system and zero were developed. Nalanda became a great centre of learning. The Amarakosha and Dharmashastras were compiled.

Religion: Puranic Hinduism developed, with devotion to Vishnu (and his avatars), Shiva and the goddess; temple worship and image-making became central; the epics and Puranas took final form. Buddhism and Jainism continued - Nalanda was a Buddhist university and Jain councils compiled their canon at Valabhi. The Guptas, though Vaishnava (bearing the title Parama Bhagavata), tolerated other faiths. These developments laid foundations for later Indian culture.

South Asian prehistory studies human societies before extensive written records through archaeological evidence. The course stresses geography, chronology, terminology and the history of archaeological research.

Prehistory is the period before writing; protohistory refers to cultures like the Harappan, which had writing that cannot yet be read, or those known from others' written records. Prehistoric archaeology relies on stone tools, bones, pollen, cave sites, rock art and dating methods such as radiocarbon (C-14), thermoluminescence and potassium-argon dating, as well as stratigraphy (the study of layers).

Robert Bruce Foote, a geologist of the Geological Survey of India, discovered the first Palaeolithic tool in India at Pallavaram near Madras in 1863, and is called the father of Indian prehistory. Major prehistoric regions include the Soan valley (Pakistan), the Narmada and Son valleys, Bhimbetka in Madhya Pradesh (with rock shelters and paintings, a UNESCO World Heritage site), Attirampakkam in Tamil Nadu and Hunsgi-Baichbal in Karnataka.
Terms such as Palaeolithic, Mesolithic and Neolithic classify broad technological and economic phases. Their dates and characteristics can vary across regions.

Palaeolithic (Old Stone Age; Greek palaios = old, lithos = stone) is subdivided into Lower, Middle and Upper phases based on tool types. Mesolithic (Middle Stone Age) is characterised by microliths (very small stone tools). Neolithic (New Stone Age, a term used by John Lubbock in 1865) is marked by polished stone tools, agriculture, animal domestication, pottery and village settlements. The Chalcolithic (copper-stone) phase followed, in which copper was used alongside stone.

Approximate dates in South Asia: Lower Palaeolithic from about 1.5 million years ago (Attirampakkam may be even older) to about 300,000-250,000 years ago; Middle Palaeolithic from about 300,000 to 40,000 years ago; Upper Palaeolithic from about 40,000 to 10,000 years ago; Mesolithic from about 10,000 to 4,000 BCE in many areas; Neolithic from about 7000 BCE at Mehrgarh, but much later in South India and the north-east. These dates overlap and vary by region.
South Asia includes diverse landscapes such as mountains, river plains, plateaus, deserts and coastal regions. Geography strongly influenced prehistoric settlement and subsistence.

Major regions: the Himalayas and north-western mountains, which form a barrier with passes such as the Khyber and Bolan that allowed migration and trade; the Indo-Gangetic plains, with fertile alluvium; the Thar desert; the Deccan plateau, with volcanic black soils and rivers such as the Godavari and Krishna; the Western and Eastern Ghats; the coastal plains; and the north-eastern hills and Brahmaputra valley, linked to Southeast Asia.

Prehistoric people chose sites near water sources and raw materials such as quartzite, chert and basalt for tools. River valleys like the Narmada, Son and Belan were rich in early sites. The monsoon climate controlled rainfall and vegetation. The diversity of environments explains why prehistoric cultures in different regions developed differently - for example, early farming in the Baluchistan hills and later Neolithic cultures in the Ganga valley and south.
Environmental changes during the last 10,000 years affected resources, settlement patterns and ways of life across South Asia.

The last 10,000 years correspond to the Holocene epoch, which began after the last Ice Age (the Pleistocene ended about 11,700 years ago). Warmer temperatures, rising sea levels and stronger monsoons in the early Holocene created more favourable conditions for plants and animals. This helped the transition from hunting-gathering to food production in places like Mehrgarh.

Climatic fluctuations continued: a period of weakening monsoons around 4,200 years ago (the '4.2 kiloyear event') is linked by many scientists to the decline of the Harappan cities. Changing river courses, such as the drying of the Ghaggar-Hakra, also affected settlement. Evidence comes from pollen analysis from lakes in Rajasthan, sediment cores and stable isotope studies. Environmental change thus shaped the timing and form of cultural change.
South Asia contains several major linguistic families. Their distribution forms part of the region's long cultural history.

The main language families of South Asia are: (1) Indo-European, especially its Indo-Aryan branch (Hindi, Bengali, Punjabi, Marathi, Gujarati, Sanskrit) and Iranian languages (Pashto, Baluchi), spoken by the majority; (2) Dravidian (Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam, and Brahui in Baluchistan, Gondi and Kurukh in central India); (3) Austroasiatic, including Munda languages (Santhali, Mundari, Ho) and Khasi in Meghalaya; and (4) Tibeto-Burman (Sino-Tibetan), spoken in the Himalayas and the north-east, including Mizo, Manipuri (Meitei), Bodo, Naga languages and Newari. Burushaski is an isolate.

The distribution suggests a long history of migrations and interactions. Dravidian may once have been spoken more widely (as Brahui shows); some scholars link the Harappan script to a proto-Dravidian language. Indo-Aryan probably arrived in the second millennium BCE. Austroasiatic may be linked with early farming in eastern India, and Tibeto-Burman speakers came from the east. Mizo belongs to the Kuki-Chin group of Tibeto-Burman languages.
Archaeological research in South Asia developed partly within colonial institutions and was shaped by the priorities and assumptions of its time.

Early interest in India's past came from European travellers and the Asiatic Society of Bengal, founded by William Jones in 1784. James Prinsep deciphered Brahmi in 1837. Alexander Cunningham, called the father of Indian archaeology, became the first Director General of the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI), founded in 1861; he surveyed sites associated with Buddhist pilgrims' accounts. Lord Curzon revived the ASI and passed the Ancient Monuments Preservation Act (1904). Under John Marshall the Indus civilisation was discovered (1920s), and Mortimer Wheeler (DG 1944-1948) introduced scientific stratigraphic excavation.

Colonial archaeology was shaped by imperial interests: it focused on monuments, Buddhist and classical sites and texts; it sometimes interpreted Indian history through racial theories (such as the Aryan invasion) and diffusionism (assuming that civilisation came from outside); and it served to present Britain as the protector of India's heritage. At the same time it laid the institutional foundation of Indian archaeology.
After independence and Partition, archaeological institutions and research developed within new national contexts and expanded regional investigation.

Partition (1947) divided many sites: Harappa and Mohenjo-daro went to Pakistan, so Indian archaeologists searched intensively for Harappan sites in India, discovering Lothal, Kalibangan, Dholavira, Rakhigarhi and others. Pakistan established its own Department of Archaeology and studied sites like Mehrgarh (excavated by French archaeologists from 1974). Universities such as Deccan College (Pune), Allahabad, Baroda and Banaras developed research programmes, and Bangladesh and Sri Lanka developed their own institutions.

Postcolonial archaeology broadened focus from monuments to settlements, ecology, technology and ordinary people's lives. Scientific methods (radiocarbon dating, archaeobotany, archaeozoology, DNA) were introduced. H. D. Sankalia (prehistory), B. B. Lal and many others led research. Debates include questions of nationalism in interpretation, such as the Saraswati river and the Aryan issue, so archaeology still needs critical, evidence-based study.
The Lower Palaeolithic represents early stone-tool traditions and very long periods of human activity in South Asia.

The Lower Palaeolithic is characterised by large core tools - handaxes and cleavers of the Acheulian tradition and choppers and chopping tools associated with the Soanian tradition of the Soan valley (Pakistan). These were made by Homo erectus or related early humans, who lived by hunting and gathering. Sites include Attirampakkam (Tamil Nadu, dated to about 1.5 million years ago), Isampur in the Hunsgi valley (Karnataka), the Narmada valley, Didwana (Rajasthan), Bhimbetka and the Belan valley (Uttar Pradesh).

Hominin remains are rare; the most important is the Hathnora skull from the Narmada valley (discovered by Arun Sonakia in 1982), variously classified as Homo erectus or archaic Homo sapiens. These people lived in open-air sites near rivers and in caves, and quartzite was a common raw material.
The Middle Palaeolithic is distinguished through changes in stone-tool technologies and archaeological assemblages.

The Middle Palaeolithic is marked by tools made on flakes struck from prepared cores, including scrapers, points and borers, using techniques like the Levallois method. Tools were smaller and lighter than in the Lower Palaeolithic, and finer-grained stones such as chert and jasper were used. H. D. Sankalia identified this phase in the Pravara valley at Nevasa (Maharashtra) and called it the 'Nevasan' culture.

Sites are found across India, including the Narmada and Son valleys, Bhimbetka, Didwana and the Luni valley of Rajasthan, and Attirampakkam, where recent research (2018) dated Middle Palaeolithic tools to about 385,000 years ago - earlier than expected and before the generally accepted arrival of modern humans. This suggests that technological change may have been developed locally.
The Upper Palaeolithic represents later Palaeolithic developments and forms part of the study of changing human behaviour and technology.

The Upper Palaeolithic is associated with anatomically modern humans (Homo sapiens). Tools include blades (long, parallel-sided flakes) and burins (chisel-like tools), along with bone tools. People made ornaments such as ostrich eggshell beads (found at Patne in Maharashtra and many sites in Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan) and may have started early art.

Important sites: Belan valley (Uttar Pradesh), the Son valley (Baghor, where a stone platform interpreted as a shrine was found), Patne, Bhimbetka, Renigunta (Andhra) and the Kurnool caves (with animal bones). The period coincided with the cold and dry conditions of the last Ice Age. Greater technological variety suggests more complex behaviour, social organisation and symbolic thinking.
The Mesolithic is associated with microlithic technologies and changing subsistence and settlement patterns after the Palaeolithic.

Microliths are tiny stone tools, often less than 5 cm, made from chert, chalcedony and other fine stones, and shaped as blades, triangles, crescents (lunates) and trapezes. They were fixed onto wooden or bone handles to make composite tools such as arrows, harpoons and sickles. The Mesolithic coincides with the warmer Holocene and shows hunting of smaller animals, fishing, gathering and, in some places, early domestication of animals.

Important sites: Bagor (Rajasthan) and Adamgarh (Madhya Pradesh), with early evidence of domesticated animals; Langhnaj (Gujarat); Sarai Nahar Rai, Mahadaha and Damdama in the Ganga plain, with burials; Bhimbetka, with many paintings of hunting, dancing and animals; and the Teri sites of Tamil Nadu. Mesolithic rock art provides vivid evidence of daily life and beliefs.
Palaeoanthropology studies human origins and populations through fossil, archaeological and related evidence. The peopling of South Asia is studied as a long process.

Modern humans (Homo sapiens) evolved in Africa about 300,000 years ago. The 'Out of Africa' theory holds that they migrated to other continents; South Asia was an important corridor, possibly along the coast of the Arabian Sea, sometime between about 70,000 and 50,000 years ago (some evidence, such as tools at Jwalapuram in Andhra Pradesh found below the ash of the Toba volcanic eruption 74,000 years ago, suggests earlier arrival).
