They owned large amounts of land (devadana), cattle and gold received as donations; employed priests, musicians, dancers (devadasis), cooks, gardeners, craftsmen and accountants; and leased land to cultivators. The Thanjavur temple inscription lists hundreds of employees.

Temples acted as banks, lending money and receiving deposits; they were centres of education (with schools and libraries), culture (music, dance, drama, festivals), and of redistribution, feeding pilgrims and the poor. They also legitimised royal authority: kings built grand temples to display their power and divine favour. Temple towns such as Kanchipuram, Thanjavur, Madurai and Chidambaram became urban centres.

sections.title: Rise and Spread of Islam
context: HIST 105 – HISTORY OF INDIA: REGIONAL KINGDOMS AND THE SULTANATE PERIOD

blocks.text: Islam emerged in Arabia in the seventh century and spread through conquest, trade and religious networks. Indian Ocean connections were important in contacts with India.

Islam was founded by the Prophet Muhammad (570-632 CE) in Arabia. In 622 CE he migrated from Mecca to Medina (the Hijra, which begins the Islamic calendar). The Quran and the five pillars - shahada (declaration of faith), salat (prayer), zakat (charity), sawm (fasting in Ramadan) and hajj (pilgrimage to Mecca) - form the basis of the faith.

After his death, the Caliphs (Rashidun, then Umayyad and Abbasid) expanded rapidly from Spain to Central Asia. Arab traders had long sailed to India's western coast; Muslim traders settled peacefully in Kerala (the Mappilas) and Gujarat. The Cheraman Juma Masjid at Kodungallur is traditionally considered one of the earliest mosques in India. Islam thus came to India both through trade and later through conquest.

sections.title: Arab Invasion of Sind
context: HIST 105 – HISTORY OF INDIA: REGIONAL KINGDOMS AND THE SULTANATE PERIOD

blocks.text: The Arab conquest of Sind created an early Muslim political presence in the subcontinent.

In 712 CE, Muhammad bin Qasim, a young Arab general sent by the Umayyad governor of Iraq, al-Hajjaj, conquered Sindh, defeating its ruler Raja Dahir. The immediate cause was the seizure of Arab ships by pirates near Debal and Dahir's refusal to punish them. The conquest is described in the 'Chachnama', a Persian text of the thirteenth century.

Sindh and Multan were ruled by Arab governors. Effects: politically limited, as the Arabs did not expand far into India (the Pratiharas and Chalukyas checked them), but culturally important. Indian knowledge of mathematics (the numerals, called 'Hindu numerals' by Arabs), astronomy (Brahmagupta's works were translated into Arabic) and medicine (Charaka, Sushruta) spread to the Arab world and later to Europe. The Hindu population was given the status of protected people (dhimmis) on paying jizya.

sections.title: Ghaznavid Invasions
context: HIST 105 – HISTORY OF INDIA: REGIONAL KINGDOMS AND THE SULTANATE PERIOD

blocks.text: Mahmud of Ghazni conducted repeated campaigns into the Indian subcontinent. Their political and economic impact forms part of early medieval history.

Mahmud of Ghazni (r. 998-1030), ruler of a Turkish kingdom in Afghanistan, invaded India about seventeen times between 1000 and 1027 CE. He defeated the Hindu Shahi ruler Jayapala (1001) and his son Anandapala, and raided wealthy temple cities such as Nagarkot, Thanesar, Mathura, Kannauj (1018) and Somnath (1025), carrying back enormous wealth.

His aims were mainly to gain wealth to finance his Central Asian wars, along with the prestige of a ghazi (warrior for Islam); he annexed only Punjab. Effects: the destruction of temples and loss of wealth, the weakening of north Indian kingdoms, the exposure of the military weakness of Indian rulers, and the incorporation of Punjab into the Ghaznavid empire, with Lahore as a centre of Persian culture. The scholar Al-Biruni accompanied Mahmud and wrote 'Kitab-ul-Hind', an important account of Indian society, religion and science.

sections.title: Ghurid Invasion
context: HIST 105 – HISTORY OF INDIA: REGIONAL KINGDOMS AND THE SULTANATE PERIOD

blocks.text: Ghurid expansion in north India helped create the political conditions for the establishment of the Delhi Sultanate.

Muhammad of Ghur (Shihabuddin Muhammad Ghori) conquered Multan (1175) and Punjab from the Ghaznavids. He was defeated by the Chalukya ruler of Gujarat (1178) and by Prithviraj Chauhan of Ajmer and Delhi in the First Battle of Tarain (1191), but defeated and killed Prithviraj in the Second Battle of Tarain (1192). He then defeated Jaichand of Kannauj at Chandawar (1194).

His general Qutbuddin Aibak conquered much of north India, and another general, Bakhtiyar Khalji, conquered Bihar and Bengal (c. 1202-1204), destroying Nalanda and Vikramashila. Unlike Mahmud, Muhammad Ghori aimed at permanent rule. After he was assassinated in 1206, Aibak became the first Sultan of Delhi. Reasons for the Turkish success included superior cavalry and military organisation, the use of mounted archers, and the political divisions among Rajput rulers.

sections.title: Delhi Sultanate
context: HIST 105 – HISTORY OF INDIA: REGIONAL KINGDOMS AND THE SULTANATE PERIOD

blocks.text: The Delhi Sultanate was a major medieval political system centred on Delhi and ruled by successive dynasties.

The Delhi Sultanate (1206-1526) was ruled by five dynasties: the Mamluk or Slave dynasty (1206-1290; Qutbuddin Aibak, Iltutmish, Razia Sultan, Balban); the Khaljis (1290-1320; Jalaluddin, Alauddin); the Tughlaqs (1320-1414; Ghiyasuddin, Muhammad bin Tughlaq, Firuz Shah); the Sayyids (1414-1451); and the Lodis (1451-1526; Bahlul, Sikandar, Ibrahim), who were Afghans.

Iltutmish consolidated the Sultanate, received recognition from the Abbasid Caliph and introduced the iqta system and the silver tanka and copper jital. Razia was the only woman ruler. Balban emphasised the divine theory of kingship. Alauddin defeated Mongol invasions and expanded into the Deccan through Malik Kafur. Muhammad bin Tughlaq ruled the largest empire. The Sultanate ended when Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi at the First Battle of Panipat (1526).

sections.title: Sultanate Administration
context: HIST 105 – HISTORY OF INDIA: REGIONAL KINGDOMS AND THE SULTANATE PERIOD

blocks.text: Administration involved the sultan, military and civil officials, revenue arrangements and territorial assignments.

The Sultan was the head of state, theoretically under the authority of the Caliph and Islamic law (Sharia). Central ministers included the wazir (finance, head of the diwan-i-wizarat), the ariz-i-mumalik (military department, diwan-i-arz), the diwan-i-insha (royal correspondence), the diwan-i-risalat (religious affairs) and the sadr-us-sudur and qazi (justice). The Turkish nobles called the Chihalgani or 'Forty' were powerful under Iltutmish until Balban crushed them.

The iqta system assigned the revenue of a territory (iqta) to an officer (muqti or iqtadar) in return for maintaining troops and administering the area; iqtas were transferable and not hereditary in principle. Provinces were later called wilayats, and below them were shiqs and parganas. Land revenue (kharaj) was the main tax; others included jizya on non-Muslims, zakat on Muslims and khams (one-fifth of war booty).

sections.title: Sultanate Architecture
context: HIST 105 – HISTORY OF INDIA: REGIONAL KINGDOMS AND THE SULTANATE PERIOD

blocks.text: The period saw new architectural forms and the interaction of different building traditions.

Sultanate architecture introduced the true arch, dome, minaret and use of lime mortar, with decoration through calligraphy, geometric patterns and arabesques (since human figures were avoided). Early buildings used materials from destroyed temples and Indian craftsmen, producing an Indo-Islamic style.

Major monuments include the Quwwat-ul-Islam mosque and the Qutb Minar (begun by Aibak, completed by Iltutmish) in Delhi; the Adhai Din ka Jhonpra in Ajmer; the tomb of Iltutmish; the Alai Darwaza (1311) built by Alauddin, the first building with a true dome and arches; Siri Fort; the sloping walls of Tughlaqabad and the tomb of Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq; Firuz Shah's Kotla; and the octagonal tombs of the Sayyids and Lodis (Lodi Gardens). Regional styles developed in Bengal, Gujarat, Jaunpur, Malwa (Mandu) and the Deccan (Gulbarga, Bidar, Bijapur).

sections.title: Sultanate Society and Economy
context: HIST 105 – HISTORY OF INDIA: REGIONAL KINGDOMS AND THE SULTANATE PERIOD

blocks.text: Agriculture formed the economic base, while towns, crafts and trade were also important. Society included diverse religious, occupational and social groups.

Society: the ruling class consisted of Turkish, Persian and later Afghan and Indian Muslim nobles (umara), along with the ulema (religious scholars). Hindu chiefs, zamindars, rais and ranas continued to hold local power. The majority were peasants, artisans and labourers. Slavery was common, and slaves could rise to high positions. Women generally faced restrictions such as purdah among the elite.

Economy: agriculture was the base, with the state claiming up to half the produce under Alauddin. New crafts (paper-making, the spinning wheel, carpet weaving) and technologies such as the Persian wheel (rahat) for irrigation spread. Towns such as Delhi, Lahore, Multan, Cambay and Daulatabad grew. Coinage standardised with the silver tanka and copper jital. Trade connected India with Central Asia, Persia and the Arab world, and Gujarati and Bengali ports thrived.

sections.title: Feudalism in South India
context: HIST 105 – HISTORY OF INDIA: REGIONAL KINGDOMS AND THE SULTANATE PERIOD

blocks.text: The concept of feudalism is used in debates about land rights, political authority and social relations in medieval South India.

Some historians applied the concept of feudalism to medieval South India, pointing to land grants (brahmadeya, devadana), the power of local chiefs and the obligations of peasants. Others rejected it. Burton Stein proposed the 'segmentary state' model for the Chola kingdom: the king had real power only in the core region; elsewhere he had only ritual sovereignty, and local peasant assemblies (nadus) and Brahmana villages were largely autonomous.

Historians such as Noboru Karashima, Y. Subbarayalu and R. Champakalakshmi criticised the segmentary model, showing evidence of Chola land surveys, revenue officials and centralised control. For Vijayanagara, the nayankara system - in which military chiefs (nayakas) received territories (amaram) in return for military service - has been compared to feudalism. The debate shows that European concepts should be applied cautiously.

sections.title: Vijayanagara Kingdom
context: HIST 105 – HISTORY OF INDIA: REGIONAL KINGDOMS AND THE SULTANATE PERIOD

blocks.text: Vijayanagara became a major South Indian empire and an important centre of political, economic and cultural life.

The Vijayanagara empire was founded in 1336 by Harihara and Bukka of the Sangama dynasty, traditionally with the guidance of the sage Vidyaranya, with its capital at Vijayanagara (Hampi) on the Tungabhadra. Four dynasties ruled: Sangama, Saluva, Tuluva and Aravidu. The greatest ruler was Krishnadevaraya (1509-1529) of the Tuluva dynasty, a great military leader and Telugu poet (author of 'Amuktamalyada'), whose court had the 'Ashtadiggajas' (eight great poets).

The empire's administration included the nayankara system (military chiefs holding amaram lands) and the ayagar system (village servants). Foreign travellers - Ibn Battuta, Abdur Razzaq (Persia), Nicolo de Conti (Italy), Domingo Paes and Fernao Nuniz (Portugal) - described its wealth. The empire was defeated at the Battle of Talikota (Rakshasa-Tangadi) in 1565 by the combined Deccan Sultanates, and the capital was destroyed. Hampi's ruins (Vitthala and Virupaksha temples) are a World Heritage site.

sections.title: Bahmani Sultanate
context: HIST 105 – HISTORY OF INDIA: REGIONAL KINGDOMS AND THE SULTANATE PERIOD

blocks.text: The Bahmani Sultanate was a major Deccan state and an important rival and contemporary of Vijayanagara.

The Bahmani Sultanate was founded in 1347 by Alauddin Hasan Bahman Shah, who rebelled against Muhammad bin Tughlaq, with its capital at Gulbarga and later Bidar. Its most famous minister was Mahmud Gawan (1460s-1481), a Persian who reformed administration, reorganised provinces (tarafs), measured land, built a madrasa at Bidar and won wars against Vijayanagara and Orissa. His execution in 1481 led to decline.

The nobility was divided between Deccanis (local Muslims and Abyssinians) and Afaqis (foreigners, mostly Persians and Turks), which weakened the state. By 1527 it split into five sultanates: Bijapur (Adil Shahis), Ahmadnagar (Nizam Shahis), Golconda (Qutb Shahis), Berar (Imad Shahis) and Bidar (Barid Shahis). The Bahmanis fought Vijayanagara repeatedly over the fertile Raichur doab between the Krishna and Tungabhadra rivers.

sections.title: Bhakti Movement
context: HIST 105 – HISTORY OF INDIA: REGIONAL KINGDOMS AND THE SULTANATE PERIOD

blocks.text: Bhakti traditions emphasised personal devotion and developed in different regional and religious forms.

Bhakti (devotion) began in South India with the Tamil Alvars (devotees of Vishnu, such as Andal, the woman saint, and Nammalvar) and Nayanars (devotees of Shiva, such as Appar, Sambandar and Sundarar) from the sixth to ninth centuries. Philosophers such as Ramanuja (vishishtadvaita) gave it a theological basis. The Virashaiva or Lingayat movement of Basavanna (twelfth century, Karnataka) rejected caste and ritual.

In north India, from the fourteenth to sixteenth centuries, saints included Ramananda, Kabir (a weaver who rejected both Hindu and Muslim formalism and preached a formless god), Guru Nanak (founder of Sikhism), Ravidas, Chaitanya (Krishna devotion in Bengal), Mirabai, Surdas and Tulsidas; in Maharashtra, Namdev, Jnaneshwar, Eknath and Tukaram; in Assam, Sankardeva. Common features: devotion to a personal god, equality before god, criticism of caste and ritual, and use of regional languages, enriching vernacular literatures.

sections.title: Sufi Movement
context: HIST 105 – HISTORY OF INDIA: REGIONAL KINGDOMS AND THE SULTANATE PERIOD

blocks.text: Sufi traditions emphasised spiritual discipline and devotion and contributed to religious and cultural life in medieval India.

Sufism is the mystical tradition of Islam, emphasising love of God, renunciation, devotion and service to humanity. Sufis were organised into silsilas (orders) led by a pir or shaikh, with disciples (murids), and lived in khanqahs (hospices). Practices included zikr (remembrance of God) and sama (devotional music, including qawwali).

Major orders in India: the Chishti silsila, founded in India by Khwaja Muinuddin Chishti of Ajmer (died 1236), with Bakhtiyar Kaki, Baba Farid and Nizamuddin Auliya of Delhi (whose disciple was the poet Amir Khusrau); the Chishtis kept away from the court. The Suhrawardi order (Bahauddin Zakariya of Multan) accepted royal grants. Later orders were the Qadiri and Naqshbandi. Sufis spread Islam peacefully, interacted with bhakti saints and developed shared shrines (dargahs) visited by people of all faiths.

sections.title: Portuguese in India
context: HIST 105 – HISTORY OF INDIA: REGIONAL KINGDOMS AND THE SULTANATE PERIOD

blocks.text: The arrival of the Portuguese by sea at the end of the fifteenth century changed maritime trade and introduced a new European political and commercial presence.

Vasco da Gama reached Calicut on the Malabar coast in May 1498, after sailing around the Cape of Good Hope, and was received by the Zamorin. The Portuguese sought direct access to spices, especially pepper, and to break the Arab and Venetian monopoly. Francisco de Almeida (first viceroy, 1505) adopted the 'blue water policy' of naval supremacy; Afonso de Albuquerque captured Goa from Bijapur in 1510, which became their capital.

They established the 'cartaz' system, requiring Asian ships to buy Portuguese passes, and built forts at Cochin, Daman, Diu, Bassein and Hooghly. They introduced new crops - tobacco, potato, chilli, maize, pineapple, cashew - and the printing press (Goa, 1556), and spread Catholic Christianity (Francis Xavier). Their power declined in the seventeenth century in the face of the Dutch and English, though they retained Goa, Daman and Diu until 1961.

sections.title: LONG NOTES
context: HIST 105 – HISTORY OF INDIA: REGIONAL KINGDOMS AND THE SULTANATE PERIOD

sections.title: Regional Kingdoms after the Guptas
context: HIST 105 – HISTORY OF INDIA: REGIONAL KINGDOMS AND THE SULTANATE PERIOD

blocks.text:
After the Gupta period, political power was distributed among regional kingdoms. Harshavardhana became an important ruler in northern India, while the Palas, Gurjara-Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas later competed in the Tripartite Struggle for Kannauj.

In eastern India, Bhaskara Varman of Kamarupa was a significant contemporary ruler. Hiuen Tsang's travel account provides valuable evidence about the political, social and religious world of the period.

Post-Gupta north India: Harshavardhana (606-647) unified much of north India from Kannauj, but his empire collapsed after his death. His reign is known from Banabhatta's Harshacharita and Hiuen Tsang's account. He was a patron of Buddhism and learning; his administration relied on feudatories and land grants. Pulakeshin II of the Chalukyas checked his southward expansion. In the east, Bhaskaravarman of Kamarupa was Harsha's ally against Shashanka of Gauda and hosted Hiuen Tsang.

Tripartite struggle (eighth-tenth centuries): the Pratiharas, Palas and Rashtrakutas fought for Kannauj. The Palas (Gopala, Dharmapala, Devapala) were patrons of Buddhism and founded Vikramashila; the Pratiharas (Nagabhata, Mihira Bhoja) defended India from Arab invasions from Sindh; the Rashtrakutas (Krishna I, who built the Kailasa temple at Ellora; Amoghavarsha) were powerful in the Deccan. The struggle weakened all three and led to the rise of Rajput kingdoms such as the Chauhans, Paramaras, Chandellas and Gahadavalas.

Hiuen Tsang's account describes: prosperity of Kannauj, Harsha's charity, the Kannauj and Prayaga assemblies, Nalanda university, caste and untouchability, the decline of Buddhism in some areas and the insecurity of roads. Historians use it with care because the pilgrim had a Buddhist perspective and favoured Harsha.

sections.title: South India and the Rise of Islam
context: HIST 105 – HISTORY OF INDIA: REGIONAL KINGDOMS AND THE SULTANATE PERIOD

blocks.text:
The Pallavas and Cholas were major South Indian powers. Temples played religious, economic, social and political roles and could become centres of land, labour and local authority.

Islam arose in Arabia and spread into wider trade and political networks. The Arab conquest of Sind established an early Muslim political presence, while later Ghaznavid campaigns connected north-western India with new political forces.

South India: the Pallavas (Kanchi) and the Chalukyas of Badami fought repeatedly in the sixth to eighth centuries; Narasimhavarman I captured Badami. Pallava art evolved from rock-cut caves to rathas and structural temples (Mamallapuram, Kailasanatha). The imperial Cholas (ninth-thirteenth centuries) under Rajaraja I and Rajendra I built a large empire including Sri Lanka and conducted naval expeditions to Southeast Asia. Their administration featured local self-government through the ur, sabha and nagaram assemblies (Uttaramerur inscriptions).

Temples: under the Pallavas and Cholas, temples became centres of economic, social and cultural life - landowners, employers, bankers, schools, centres of art and music and symbols of royal power. The Brihadeshvara temple at Thanjavur and the Gangaikondacholapuram temple are outstanding examples. Bronze images (Nataraja) and the Bhakti hymns of the Alvars and Nayanars were connected with temple worship.

Islam: founded in seventh-century Arabia, it reached India through Arab traders on the Malabar coast and Gujarat, and through the Arab conquest of Sindh in 712 by Muhammad bin Qasim. The Arab conquest was limited but led to cultural exchange of Indian sciences with the Arab world. The Ghaznavid raids (Mahmud of Ghazni, 1000-1027) plundered temples such as Somnath and annexed Punjab; Al-Biruni's Kitab-ul-Hind recorded Indian society. The Ghurid conquest (Tarain 1192) led to permanent rule.

sections.title: Delhi Sultanate
context: HIST 105 – HISTORY OF INDIA: REGIONAL KINGDOMS AND THE SULTANATE PERIOD

blocks.text:
The Ghurid invasions prepared the way for the establishment of the Delhi Sultanate. The Sultanate developed administrative structures based on monarchy, officials, military organisation, revenue collection and territorial control.

The period also witnessed important developments in architecture and literature. Agriculture remained central to the economy, while towns, crafts and commerce contributed to economic life. Society was diverse and changed through political and cultural interaction.

Establishment: after Muhammad Ghori's victories (Tarain 1192, Chandawar 1194) and his death (1206), Qutbuddin Aibak founded the Sultanate. Iltutmish (1211-1236) consolidated it, organised the iqta system and the Forty, introduced the tanka and jital and obtained recognition from the Caliph. Balban (1266-1287) strengthened royal power (theory of kingship, sijda and paibos, spy system) and defended against the Mongols. Alauddin Khalji (1296-1316) defeated the Mongols, conquered Gujarat, Ranthambhor, Chittor and Malwa and sent Malik Kafur to the Deccan and far south. Muhammad bin Tughlaq (1325-1351) attempted bold experiments; Firuz Shah Tughlaq (1351-1388) focused on public works and welfare. The Lodis were the last dynasty.

Administration: the Sultan held supreme authority; ministers headed the diwan-i-wizarat, diwan-i-arz, diwan-i-insha and diwan-i-risalat; the iqta system linked revenue with military service; provinces and local units were administered by iqtadars and local officials; and Hindu chiefs often retained local power as tributaries. Justice was administered by qazis according to Sharia and custom.

Culture and society: Indo-Islamic architecture (Qutb Minar, Alai Darwaza, Tughlaqabad), Persian literature (Amir Khusrau, historians Minhaj-us-Siraj, Ziauddin Barani), the development of Hindavi/Urdu, music (Khusrau's contributions), Sufi and Bhakti movements. Economy: agricultural base with heavy revenue under Alauddin, growth of towns, crafts (paper, textiles), Persian wheel irrigation, and trade with Central and West Asia. Society included Turkish and Indian Muslim elites, Hindu chiefs, peasants, artisans and slaves.

sections.title: Supra-Regional Kingdoms, Bhakti, Sufism and Portuguese Arrival
context: HIST 105 – HISTORY OF INDIA: REGIONAL KINGDOMS AND THE SULTANATE PERIOD

blocks.text:
Vijayanagara and the Bahmani Sultanate became major political powers in South India and the Deccan. Historians also debate the usefulness of feudalism for understanding medieval South Indian political and agrarian relations.

Bhakti and Sufi traditions transformed religious life through varied forms of devotion and spiritual practice. At the end of the fifteenth century, Portuguese arrival by sea altered Indian Ocean commerce and began a new phase of European involvement in India.

Vijayanagara and Bahmani: founded in 1336 and 1347 respectively, they fought for control of the Raichur doab and the ports of the western coast. Vijayanagara reached its peak under Krishnadevaraya (1509-1529), with a strong army, the nayankara system and a magnificent capital at Hampi described by foreign travellers. The Bahmani Sultanate prospered under Mahmud Gawan but split into five sultanates by 1527. The Deccan Sultanates jointly defeated Vijayanagara at Talikota (1565).

Feudalism debate: historians have applied the concept to land grants and local chiefs. Burton Stein's segmentary state theory (for the Cholas and Vijayanagara) argued that royal power was limited outside the core; others (Karashima, Subbarayalu) emphasised centralised features. The nayankara system has been compared to European feudalism but differed in many ways.

Religious movements: Bhakti saints (Alvars and Nayanars in the south; Kabir, Nanak, Chaitanya, Mirabai, Tulsidas in the north; Tukaram and Namdev in Maharashtra; Sankardeva in Assam) emphasised personal devotion and equality and used vernacular languages. Sufis (Chishti, Suhrawardi, Qadiri and Naqshbandi orders) promoted love of God and humanity and created syncretic traditions. Together they promoted tolerance, social reform and regional literature.

Portuguese arrival: Vasco da Gama reached Calicut in 1498. The Portuguese captured Goa (1510), set up forts and the cartaz system to control Indian Ocean trade, introduced new crops and printing and spread Christianity. Their arrival marked the beginning of European colonial involvement in India.

sections.title: HIST 106 – INDIA AND SOUTHEAST ASIA (MAJOR OPTIONAL)
SHORT NOTES
context: HIST 106 – INDIA AND SOUTHEAST ASIA (MAJOR OPTIONAL)

sections.title: Ancient Trade Routes
context: HIST 106 – INDIA AND SOUTHEAST ASIA (MAJOR OPTIONAL)

blocks.text: India and Southeast Asia were connected through maritime routes including networks described in the syllabus as the Maritime Silk Road and Spice Route.

India and Southeast Asia were linked by sea across the Bay of Bengal. Sailors used the monsoon winds, sailing east from Indian ports such as Tamralipti (Bengal), Puhar (Kaveripattinam) and Arikamedu (Tamil Nadu) and Kalinga (Odisha) to Southeast Asian ports, then onward through the Strait of Malacca to China. Indian literature calls Southeast Asia 'Suvarnabhumi' (land of gold) and 'Suvarnadvipa' (island of gold).

The 'Maritime Silk Road' connected China, Southeast Asia, India, the Persian Gulf, Arabia and the Mediterranean, while the 'Spice Route' carried pepper, cloves, nutmeg and cinnamon from India, the Moluccas and Sri Lanka. Archaeological evidence includes Indian beads, pottery (rouletted ware) and seals at sites such as Ban Don Ta Phet (Thailand), Oc Eo (Vietnam) and Khao Sam Kaeo (Thailand). Odisha's Bali Jatra festival commemorates ancient voyages to Bali.

sections.title: Indian Traders
context: HIST 106 – INDIA AND SOUTHEAST ASIA (MAJOR OPTIONAL)

blocks.text: Indian merchants participated in long-distance exchange and helped carry religious and cultural ideas across maritime networks.

Indian merchant guilds such as the Manigramam, the Ainurruvar (the 'Five Hundred' of Aihole) and the Nanadesi operated across South India, Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia from about the ninth century. A Tamil inscription of a merchant guild has been found in Sumatra (Lobu Tua, 1088 CE) and others in Thailand and Myanmar. Merchants brought textiles, beads and other goods, and returned with spices, gold, camphor, sandalwood and aromatic woods.

Merchants were accompanied by Brahmanas and Buddhist monks, and they built temples and monasteries. Through such contacts, Indian scripts (derived from the Pallava-Grantha script), Sanskrit and religious ideas spread. Some scholars (the 'Vaishya theory') argue that traders were the main carriers of Indian culture, while others give more importance to Brahmanas (the 'Brahmana theory') or local rulers who invited them.

sections.title: Spread of Buddhism and Hinduism
context: HIST 106 – INDIA AND SOUTHEAST ASIA (MAJOR OPTIONAL)

blocks.text: Buddhist and Hindu traditions spread into Southeast Asia through long processes involving merchants, monks, rulers and local adaptation.

Hinduism spread from the early centuries CE through Brahmanas invited by local rulers to perform rituals that legitimised kingship. Early Indianised kingdoms included Funan (Mekong delta), Champa (central Vietnam), the kingdoms of Java (Mataram), and later the Khmer empire of Cambodia. Kings took Sanskrit names ending in '-varman', used Sanskrit inscriptions (such as the Vo Canh inscription in Vietnam and the Kutai inscriptions in Borneo, about the fifth century) and worshipped Shiva, Vishnu and the devaraja (god-king).

Buddhism spread through monks and traders. Theravada Buddhism, partly through Sri Lanka, became dominant in Myanmar, Thailand, Laos and Cambodia; Mahayana and Vajrayana flourished in the Srivijaya empire (Sumatra), where the Chinese monk Yijing studied Sanskrit in the seventh century. Southeast Asians adapted these religions, combining them with local spirit and ancestor worship - a process scholars call localisation rather than simple 'Indianisation'.

sections.title: Art and Architecture
context: HIST 106 – INDIA AND SOUTHEAST ASIA (MAJOR OPTIONAL)

blocks.text: India and Southeast Asia participated in cross-cultural artistic exchange. Influences were adapted within local traditions rather than simply copied.

Southeast Asian art and architecture show Indian influence combined with local creativity. Borobudur in Java (eighth-ninth centuries), built by the Shailendra dynasty, is the world's largest Buddhist monument, shaped like a mandala with narrative reliefs. Prambanan in Java (ninth century) is a great Hindu temple complex dedicated to the Trimurti, with Ramayana reliefs. Angkor Wat in Cambodia (twelfth century), built by Suryavarman II and dedicated to Vishnu, is the largest religious monument in the world; Angkor Thom and the Bayon (Jayavarman VII) are Buddhist.

Other examples include the Cham towers of My Son (Vietnam) and the temples of Bagan (Myanmar). Ramayana stories are performed in Thai (Ramakien), Javanese (Kakawin Ramayana) and Cambodian (Reamker) versions, and in shadow puppet theatre (wayang). Scholars stress that these works are not copies but Southeast Asian creations using shared religious ideas.

sections.title: Cholas and Southeast Asia
context: HIST 106 – INDIA AND SOUTHEAST ASIA (MAJOR OPTIONAL)

blocks.text: The Cholas were involved in maritime trade and political interaction with Southeast Asia and influenced regional connections.

The Cholas had extensive maritime trade with Southeast Asia and China, carried out by Tamil merchant guilds. Relations with the Srivijaya empire were at first friendly - the Shailendra king Maravijayottungavarman built a Buddhist vihara at Nagapattinam with the permission of Rajaraja I (the Larger Leiden plates). But in 1025, Rajendra I sent a naval expedition that attacked Srivijaya and its ports, including Kadaram (Kedah, Malaysia), probably to secure trade routes against obstacles to Chola merchants.

Kulottunga I also maintained relations, and the Cholas sent embassies to the Song emperors of China. The expedition shows the importance of maritime trade to the Cholas and their naval power. Chola influence also appears in Tamil inscriptions in Southeast Asia and Hindu temples built by Tamil merchants.

sections.title: Vijayanagara and Southeast Asia
context: HIST 106 – INDIA AND SOUTHEAST ASIA (MAJOR OPTIONAL)

blocks.text: The syllabus includes Vijayanagara in examining medieval links involving religion, language and literature.

Vijayanagara (1336-1565) was a major centre of Hindu temple culture, Sanskrit, Telugu and Kannada literature and maritime trade. Its western and eastern coastal ports (such as Bhatkal and Pulicat) traded with Southeast Asia, exporting textiles and importing spices and other goods. Students should study the prescribed readings for the specific influence of Vijayanagara on religion, language and literature in Southeast Asia.

In this period, Indian connections with Southeast Asia were maintained largely through trade. Sanskrit and Tamil literary traditions continued to influence Southeast Asian courts, while Theravada Buddhism and Islam became the dominant religions in most of Southeast Asia. Vijayanagara's role should be seen as one part of continuing networks of exchange.

sections.title: Islam and Indian Ocean Trade
context: HIST 106 – INDIA AND SOUTHEAST ASIA (MAJOR OPTIONAL)

blocks.text: Islam spread through Southeast Asian maritime networks in which merchants and Indian Ocean connections played an important role.

Islam spread in Southeast Asia from about the thirteenth century, largely through Muslim traders from Gujarat, the Coromandel coast, Bengal, Arabia and Persia, and through Sufi missionaries. Marco Polo noted a Muslim town (Perlak) in Sumatra in 1292, and the tombstone of Sultan Malik al-Salih of Samudra-Pasai (1297) is early evidence. Gujarati-style gravestones are found in Pasai and Java.

The Malacca Sultanate (fifteenth century), whose ruler converted to Islam, became a centre for Islam's spread through trade. Islam spread to Java (through the Wali Songo, nine saints), the Moluccas and the southern Philippines. Today Indonesia has the world's largest Muslim population. Indian Muslim traders thus played an important role, and the spread was largely peaceful and adapted to local culture.

sections.title: British Colonialism in India
context: HIST 106 – INDIA AND SOUTHEAST ASIA (MAJOR OPTIONAL)

blocks.text: British colonialism transformed India's economy and politics and contributed to the growth of nationalism and the struggle for independence.

British rule began with the English East India Company's victory at Plassey (1757) and Buxar (1764), and after the Revolt of 1857 India came under direct Crown rule (1858). Colonial policies included land revenue settlements (Permanent, Ryotwari, Mahalwari), deindustrialisation of handicrafts, the drain of wealth to Britain, commercialisation of agriculture, railways and modern education.

These policies caused famines, poverty and resentment, but also created an educated class, communications and a unified administration. Indian nationalism developed through the Indian National Congress (1885), the moderates and extremists, the Swadeshi movement (1905), Gandhian movements (Non-Cooperation 1920-22, Civil Disobedience 1930-34, Quit India 1942) and revolutionary activity. India became independent on 15 August 1947, with partition into India and Pakistan.

sections.title: Colonialism in Southeast Asia
context: HIST 106 – INDIA AND SOUTHEAST ASIA (MAJOR OPTIONAL)

blocks.text: Dutch, French and British colonial regimes exploited labour and resources and stimulated different nationalist responses.

Colonial powers in Southeast Asia: the Dutch in the East Indies (Indonesia) from the seventeenth century, with the forced cultivation 'Cultivation System' (cultuurstelsel, 1830-1870); the Spanish and later Americans in the Philippines; the British in Burma (annexed through three wars, 1824-1885, and governed as part of British India until 1937), Malaya and Singapore (rubber and tin); and the French in Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos (French Indochina). Siam (Thailand) remained independent as a buffer state.

Nationalist responses: Indonesian nationalism (Sukarno, independence declared in 1945 and won in 1949); Vietnamese communism and nationalism under Ho Chi Minh, leading to wars against France (Dien Bien Phu, 1954) and the USA; Burmese nationalism (Aung San, independence 1948); the Philippines (Jose Rizal, independence 1946); and Malayan independence (1957). The Japanese occupation in the Second World War weakened European colonial rule. Indian nationalism inspired Southeast Asian leaders, and the Indian National Army was organised in Southeast Asia by Subhas Chandra Bose.

sections.title: Postcolonial Relations
context: HIST 106 – INDIA AND SOUTHEAST ASIA (MAJOR OPTIONAL)

blocks.text: After independence, India and Southeast Asian countries developed new diplomatic, political and cultural relationships.

After independence, India under Jawaharlal Nehru supported decolonisation in Asia: it hosted the Asian Relations Conference (1947) and a conference on Indonesia (1949), and participated in the Bandung Conference (1955), which led to the Non-Aligned Movement (1961), founded with Sukarno of Indonesia among others. During the Cold War, relations cooled as some Southeast Asian countries were aligned with the West and India had close ties with the Soviet Union.

From 1991, India's 'Look East Policy' under P. V. Narasimha Rao sought closer ties with Southeast Asia. India became a sectoral partner of ASEAN (1992), a full dialogue partner (1996), a summit-level partner (2002) and a strategic partner (2012). In 2014 it became the 'Act East Policy', emphasising connectivity (the India-Myanmar-Thailand Trilateral Highway, the Kaladan Multi-Modal Transit Transport Project through Mizoram), security and culture. North-east India, including Mizoram, is seen as the gateway to Southeast Asia.

sections.title: Economic Ties
context: HIST 106 – INDIA AND SOUTHEAST ASIA (MAJOR OPTIONAL)

blocks.text: Trade, investment and tourism are important areas of contemporary India-Southeast Asia relations.

The ASEAN-India Free Trade Agreement in goods came into force in 2010, with agreements on services and investment later. ASEAN is one of India's largest trading partners, with bilateral trade over 100 billion US dollars in recent years. Singapore is among the biggest sources of foreign direct investment into India, and Indian companies invest in Southeast Asia in IT, pharmaceuticals, automobiles and infrastructure.

Connectivity projects (roads, shipping, air links), Indian technology and education programmes, and tourism (Buddhist circuits, Southeast Asian tourists visiting Bodh Gaya, Indians travelling to Thailand, Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia) strengthen economic ties. India decided not to join the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP) in 2019, mainly due to concerns about trade deficits.

sections.title: Cultural Exchange
context: HIST 106 – INDIA AND SOUTHEAST ASIA (MAJOR OPTIONAL)

blocks.text: Modern cultural exchange includes popular culture, education and media, including the influence of Indian cinema mentioned in the syllabus.

Indian films, especially Bollywood, have long been popular in Southeast Asia, particularly in Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore and Myanmar; Indian film songs influenced local music genres such as Indonesian dangdut. Large Indian diaspora communities (especially Tamils in Malaysia, Singapore and Myanmar) maintain festivals such as Deepavali and Thaipusam.

Cultural exchange also includes Indian scholarships for Southeast Asian students, the revival of Nalanda University (2010s) with participation from East Asian countries, Ramayana festivals, yoga, Indian cuisine and Buddhist pilgrimages. The exchange runs both ways: Southeast Asian food, music, martial arts and tourism also influence India, especially the north-east.

sections.title: LONG NOTES
context: HIST 106 – INDIA AND SOUTHEAST ASIA (MAJOR OPTIONAL)

sections.title: Ancient India and Southeast Asia
context: HIST 106 – INDIA AND SOUTHEAST ASIA (MAJOR OPTIONAL)

blocks.text:
Ancient connections between India and Southeast Asia developed through maritime trade routes. Merchants, religious specialists and political elites participated in networks that carried goods and ideas.

Buddhism and Hinduism spread through these connections but were adapted by Southeast Asian societies according to local conditions. Art and architecture also show cross-cultural exchange. These relations are best understood as interaction rather than one-way cultural transfer.

Trade routes and merchants: from the early centuries BCE, Indian sailors used the monsoon to travel across the Bay of Bengal. Ports such as Tamralipti, Kaveripattinam, Arikamedu and Kalinga connected with Southeast Asian ports (Oc Eo, Khao Sam Kaeo, Ban Don Ta Phet) and further to China. The Jatakas and Sangam texts mention voyages to Suvarnabhumi. Indian goods included textiles, beads and metalware; imports included gold, spices, camphor and aromatic woods. Merchant guilds later had inscriptions in Southeast Asia.

Spread of religion: Hinduism spread through Brahmanas invited by local rulers to legitimise kingship (Funan, Champa, Java, Angkor) and Buddhism through monks and traders (Srivijaya, Myanmar, Thailand). Theories of the process include the Kshatriya theory (Indian conquest, now rejected), the Vaishya theory (traders), the Brahmana theory (priests invited by rulers) and the localisation theory (O. W. Wolters), which emphasises that Southeast Asians selected and adapted Indian ideas to their own needs.

Art and architecture: Borobudur, Prambanan, Angkor Wat, the Bayon, My Son and Bagan show Indian religious themes and architectural ideas (the mandala, the temple-mountain representing Mount Meru) adapted to local styles. Sanskrit, Pali and Indian scripts formed the basis of Southeast Asian scripts (Khmer, Thai, Javanese). The Ramayana and Mahabharata became part of local literature and theatre. These were interactions of mutual exchange, not one-way transfer.

sections.title: Medieval Connections
context: HIST 106 – INDIA AND SOUTHEAST ASIA (MAJOR OPTIONAL)

blocks.text:
During the medieval period, Indian states such as the Cholas participated in maritime networks connecting the Bay of Bengal and Southeast Asia. The syllabus also includes Vijayanagara in examining influence in religion, language and literature.

Islam spread widely in Southeast Asia through Indian Ocean commercial and religious networks. Trade therefore served as an important channel for cultural and religious interaction.

The Cholas: Tamil merchant guilds traded in Southeast Asia and China; relations with Srivijaya were initially friendly (the Nagapattinam vihara) but Rajendra I's naval expedition of 1025 attacked Kadaram and other ports to protect Chola trade. The Cholas also sent embassies to China. Tamil inscriptions in Sumatra, Thailand and Myanmar show the activities of guilds such as the Ainurruvar.

Vijayanagara: maintained ports and trade with Southeast Asia; its influence on religion, language and literature continued older traditions of Sanskrit and Tamil learning. Indian epics and Hindu-Buddhist ideas remained alive in Southeast Asian courts even as Theravada Buddhism and Islam spread.

Islam: from the thirteenth century, Gujarati, Bengali and Tamil Muslim merchants, along with Arab and Persian traders and Sufis, spread Islam to Sumatra (Samudra-Pasai), Malacca, Java and the Moluccas. Malacca became the commercial and Islamic centre in the fifteenth century. Islam adapted to local culture, with Javanese Islam retaining elements of earlier traditions. Trade networks were therefore the main channel for cultural and religious interaction in the medieval period.

sections.title: Colonialism in India and Southeast Asia
context: HIST 106 – INDIA AND SOUTHEAST ASIA (MAJOR OPTIONAL)

blocks.text:
British colonialism deeply affected India and contributed to the growth of nationalism and the independence struggle. Southeast Asia experienced Dutch, French and British colonial rule in different regions.

Colonial systems exploited resources and labour and restructured economies and administration. They also produced new political responses and nationalist movements. Comparing the two regions helps students see both shared colonial experiences and important differences.

Colonialism in India: the British East India Company conquered India from 1757 and the Crown took over in 1858. Land revenue systems, commercialisation of agriculture, deindustrialisation, the drain of wealth, famines, railways and Western education transformed the economy and society. Indian nationalism developed from the late nineteenth century, through the Congress, Gandhi's mass movements and revolutionary activities, culminating in independence in 1947.

Colonialism in Southeast Asia: the Dutch exploited Indonesia through monopolies and the Cultivation System; the French ruled Indochina, establishing plantations (rubber, rice exports); the British ruled Burma (part of British India until 1937), Malaya (rubber, tin, with Indian and Chinese immigrant labour) and Singapore. The Spanish and Americans ruled the Philippines; Siam remained independent. Indian labourers and soldiers were taken to Southeast Asia, creating diaspora communities.

Comparison: both regions experienced economic exploitation, export-oriented economies, new administrative systems, Western education and racial hierarchy. Nationalist movements arose in both, often influenced by each other - Gandhi and Nehru inspired Southeast Asian leaders, and the INA operated from Southeast Asia. Differences include the variety of colonial powers in Southeast Asia, the role of communism (Vietnam), and the effect of the Japanese occupation, which hastened decolonisation.

sections.title: Postcolonial India-Southeast Asia Relations
context: HIST 106 – INDIA AND SOUTHEAST ASIA (MAJOR OPTIONAL)

blocks.text:
After independence, India and Southeast Asian states developed new ties based on diplomacy, trade and regional cooperation. Economic relations include trade, investment and tourism.

Cultural exchanges also continue through media and popular culture. The syllabus specifically mentions Indian cinema as one influence in Southeast Asian popular culture. Modern relations therefore combine historical connections with contemporary political and economic interests.

Phase I (1947-1960s): India supported Asian independence movements (the Asian Relations Conference 1947, the Indonesia conference 1949), the Bandung Conference (1955) and the Non-Aligned Movement. Nehru and Sukarno were close allies. Phase II (1960s-1980s): relations weakened because of the Cold War, the war with China (1962), India's ties with the USSR and its support for Vietnam in Cambodia, while ASEAN (1967) countries were pro-Western.

Phase III (from 1991): the Look East Policy, India-ASEAN partnerships, the ASEAN-India FTA (2010), the East Asia Summit (from 2005) and the Act East Policy (2014). Projects include the Kaladan Multi-Modal Transit Transport Project linking Kolkata to Sittwe port in Myanmar and on to Mizoram, and the India-Myanmar-Thailand Trilateral Highway. Security cooperation includes maritime cooperation in the Indo-Pacific.

Cultural relations draw on shared heritage - Buddhism, the Ramayana, temples such as Angkor (which India helped to restore) - and on Indian cinema, diaspora and education. Mizoram and the north-east are central to the Act East Policy because of their borders with Myanmar and Bangladesh.
The Harappan economy was based on agriculture, animal husbandry, craft production and trade supported by urban settlements.

Harappan agriculture produced wheat, barley, pulses, sesame, mustard, cotton and some rice, using ploughs (Kalibangan ploughed field) and probably flood irrigation. Surplus grain was stored in large granaries. Animals included cattle, buffalo, sheep, goats and pigs; the camel and horse were rare. Crafts included bead-making, metalwork in copper and bronze, pottery, textiles and seal-making, with specialised production centres such as Chanhudaro and Lothal.

Trade was organised with standardised weights and measures and seals. Internal trade obtained raw materials (copper from Rajasthan's Khetri, lapis lazuli from Afghanistan, shells from the coast). External trade linked with Mesopotamia (Meluhha), the Persian Gulf (Dilmun) and Oman (Magan). There is no evidence of coins; exchange was probably by barter.
Pastoralism was highly important in the Early Vedic economy, though cultivation and exchange were also present.

The Rigvedic economy was primarily pastoral: cattle were the main wealth, used as a unit of value and in gifts (dakshina) to priests. Words for war (gavishti), wealthy person (gomat) and daughter (duhitri, one who milks) reflect the importance of cattle. Horses were important for chariots. There was some cultivation of barley (yava), using wooden ploughs.

Crafts included carpentry, chariot-making, metalworking (copper/bronze, ayas), weaving and leatherwork. There were no towns, coins or regular taxation; the chief received voluntary gifts (bali) and booty from raids. Trade was by barter. The economy was suited to a semi-nomadic tribal society.
Agriculture and settled territorial life became more prominent during the Later Vedic period.

In the Later Vedic period (c. 1000-600 BCE), people settled in the Ganga-Yamuna doab and moved further east. Iron (krishna ayas), introduced around 1000 BCE, provided axes and later ploughshares, which helped clear forests and expand agriculture. Crops included rice (vrihi), wheat, barley, beans and sesame; the Shatapatha Brahmana describes ploughing rituals.

Settled villages grew, associated with Painted Grey Ware. Specialised crafts and occupations increased, and the first signs of guilds appeared. Bali became a regular tax collected by the king's officer (bhagadugha). Trade expanded, and the nishka (a gold ornament) was used as a unit of value. The economy laid the basis for urbanisation.
The post-Vedic period saw expanding agriculture, towns, crafts, trade and monetary exchange alongside the rise of states.

The sixth century BCE saw a 'second urbanisation' in the Ganga valley. Iron ploughshares, wet rice cultivation (transplanting) and agricultural surplus supported a growing population. Towns such as Rajagriha, Shravasti, Kaushambi, Varanasi, Champa and Ujjain developed as political and commercial centres.

Crafts were organised in guilds (shreni) headed by the jettha; merchants (setthi) became wealthy. The first coins, silver punch-marked coins (karshapana), appeared. Trade routes such as the Uttarapatha and Dakshinapatha connected regions. Taxes became regular, and land revenue was collected by the state. Buddhist and Jain texts describe this flourishing economy and its social effects, including the growth of a merchant class that supported new religions.
Agriculture, taxation, crafts and trade supported the Mauryan Empire and linked different economic regions.

The Mauryan state played an active role in the economy, as described in the Arthashastra. Land revenue (bhaga) of usually one-sixth was the main source of income; there were also taxes on trade, crafts and irrigation (udakabhaga), and crown lands (sita) cultivated under state supervision. The state controlled mining, forests, salt, liquor and weapons manufacture.

Superintendents (adhyakshas) regulated trade, weights and measures, prices and markets. Punch-marked silver coins (pana) were widely used. Roads like the Uttarapatha linked the empire, and trade extended to Central Asia, West Asia and Sri Lanka. Irrigation works (Sudarshana lake) supported agriculture. The Mauryan economy was thus partly state-controlled and partly private.
The Gupta economy remained agrarian, while land grants, trade and coinage are important subjects of historical debate.

The Gupta economy was mainly agrarian. The state collected revenue of one-sixth or more, plus other levies and forced labour. Land grants to Brahmanas and religious institutions (agrahara, devadana) became widespread, often with fiscal and administrative rights, extending agriculture into new areas.

The Guptas issued many gold coins (dinara) and some silver and copper coins. Guilds of merchants and artisans remained important (Mandasor inscription of the silk weavers). Foreign trade with Rome declined, but trade with Southeast Asia, China and Byzantium continued. Historians debate whether this period saw a decline of towns and trade and the rise of feudalism, as argued by R. S. Sharma, or continuity and regional growth, as others argue.
Feudalism is an interpretive concept used to discuss changing land rights, political authority and agrarian relations in early medieval India.

R. S. Sharma ('Indian Feudalism', 1965) argued that from about the fourth to the twelfth centuries, land grants created landed intermediaries, peasants lost their freedom (forced labour, eviction), trade and towns declined (fewer coins, especially from 600-1000 CE), and political power was fragmented among feudatories (samantas). D. D. Kosambi had earlier distinguished 'feudalism from above' and 'feudalism from below'.

Critics argued that the model imposed a European framework; that Indian peasants were not serfs bound to land; that trade, coins and towns continued in many areas; and that land grants represented agrarian expansion and state formation. B. D. Chattopadhyaya's 'integrative polity' model and Burton Stein's segmentary state are alternatives. The concept is useful as a starting point for debate, but must be applied carefully.
Indo-Roman trade connected Indian producers and ports with Mediterranean markets.

Indo-Roman trade flourished from the first century BCE to the third century CE, after the Roman conquest of Egypt (30 BCE) and the use of the monsoon winds (Hippalus). The Periplus of the Erythraean Sea and Pliny's Natural History describe it. Major Indian ports included Barygaza (Broach), Muziris (Pattanam, Kerala), Arikamedu and Kaveripattinam.

Exports included pepper, spices, cotton textiles, precious stones, pearls, ivory, indigo and exotic animals; imports included wine, olive oil, glass, coral, tin, lead and large quantities of Roman gold and silver coins, many of which have been found in South India. Pliny complained of the drain of Roman wealth to India. The trade enriched South Indian kingdoms and the Satavahanas and stimulated crafts and urbanisation.
Indian Ocean networks connected India with West Asia, East Africa and Southeast Asia through maritime commerce.

The Indian Ocean was a vast trading zone linked by the monsoon winds. India was at its centre, connecting East Africa (gold, ivory, slaves), Arabia and the Persian Gulf (horses, dates, pearls), Southeast Asia (spices, tin, aromatic woods) and China (silk, porcelain). Indian exports included textiles (the most important), pepper, indigo, rice and precious stones.

Merchants included Gujaratis, Tamils, Chettis, Arabs, Persians, Jews and Chinese. Ports such as Cambay, Calicut, Quilon, Masulipatnam and Hooghly flourished. Trading communities settled in each other's ports, and the trade was largely peaceful until the Portuguese arrived in 1498 and tried to control it by force with the cartaz system. Later the Dutch, English and French East India Companies dominated the trade.
Alauddin Khalji is associated with market regulations and revenue measures designed partly to support the military and strengthen state control.

Alauddin Khalji (1296-1316) needed a large standing army to fight the Mongols and expand his empire, but wanted to pay soldiers low salaries. He therefore introduced market reforms described by the historian Ziauddin Barani: fixed low prices for grain, cloth, horses, cattle and slaves; four separate markets in Delhi; government granaries to store grain; officials (shahna-i-mandi for the grain market, diwan-i-riyasat) and spies to enforce the rules; and severe punishments for merchants who cheated (cutting flesh equal to the weight of short-weighed goods).

His revenue reforms included measuring land (masahat) and fixing revenue at half the produce; abolishing the privileges of intermediaries such as khuts, muqaddams and chaudharis; imposing house tax and grazing tax; and creating a department (diwan-i-mustakhraj) to recover arrears. These measures increased state revenue and kept prices low, but placed heavy burdens on peasants and did not last after his death.
Muhammad bin Tughlaq introduced ambitious fiscal and monetary experiments whose implementation created serious difficulties.

Muhammad bin Tughlaq (1325-1351) undertook several bold experiments: (1) raising taxes in the Doab (between the Ganga and Yamuna), which coincided with famine, causing revolts and peasant flight; (2) transferring the capital from Delhi to Daulatabad (Devagiri) in the Deccan in 1327, forcing people to move and later return; (3) introducing token currency of copper and brass coins (1329-1330) with the value of silver tankas, which failed because the coins were easily forged and the state had to redeem them in silver; and (4) planned expeditions to Khurasan and Qarachil (in the Himalayas), which wasted resources.

He also created a department of agriculture (diwan-i-amir-i-kohi) to expand cultivation and gave loans (sondhar) to farmers. These policies were intelligent in concept but poorly implemented and badly timed. Historians such as Barani and Ibn Battuta (who served at his court) give critical accounts. They led to rebellions and the breakaway of provinces such as Vijayanagara (1336) and the Bahmanis (1347).
The Mughal economy rested largely on agriculture and land revenue, supported by towns, crafts, internal commerce and international trade.

Agriculture was the base; the Mughals collected land revenue through the zabt system established by Akbar's minister Raja Todar Mal - land was measured, classified by fertility (polaj, parauti, chachar and banjar), and the revenue was fixed at one-third of the average produce over ten years (dahsala), payable in cash. Revenue was assigned to mansabdars as jagirs. Zamindars collected revenue locally. Cash crops such as cotton, indigo, sugarcane and tobacco expanded.

India was a major manufacturing economy, especially in textiles (Bengal muslin, Gujarat calicoes), and had large towns such as Agra, Delhi, Lahore, Surat and Dhaka. Internal trade used a network of roads, sarais and banking (hundis or bills of exchange, sarrafs or money-changers). International trade with Europe, West and Southeast Asia brought a large inflow of silver. Mughal India is estimated to have produced about a quarter of world output around 1700.
Colonial land revenue systems reshaped relations among the state, landlords and cultivators and had major effects on rural society.

The Permanent Settlement (1793) of Lord Cornwallis in Bengal, Bihar and Odisha recognised zamindars as owners of land and fixed the revenue permanently; failure to pay meant the estate was sold (Sunset Law). Peasants became tenants at the mercy of zamindars. The Ryotwari Settlement (Thomas Munro, from 1820, Madras and Bombay) made the ryot (cultivator) the owner, paying revenue directly to the state, assessed for 20-30 years and often very high. The Mahalwari Settlement (Holt Mackenzie, 1822; extended by William Bentinck, 1833, North-Western Provinces and Punjab) assessed the village (mahal) as a whole.

Effects: high revenue demand, the creation of a land market and the sale of land, the rise of absentee landlords and moneylenders, the impoverishment and indebtedness of peasants, the commercialisation of agriculture (indigo, cotton, jute) and peasant revolts such as the Indigo Revolt (1859-1860) and the Deccan Riots (1875).
Many cultivators became dependent on credit and moneylenders, making indebtedness an important feature of the colonial rural economy.

Causes: heavy and rigid land revenue demands payable in cash; frequent famines and crop failures; fragmentation of holdings; the commercialisation of agriculture, which made peasants dependent on markets and prices; the ruin of handicrafts, which forced more people onto the land; and the creation of transferable property rights, which allowed land to be mortgaged to moneylenders (sahukars, mahajans). Social expenses on marriages and ceremonies also contributed.

Moneylenders charged high interest and often took over peasants' land, turning owners into tenants or labourers. This led to the Deccan Riots of 1875, when peasants attacked moneylenders and burned their bonds. The government passed laws such as the Deccan Agriculturists' Relief Act (1879) and the Punjab Land Alienation Act (1900), and promoted cooperative credit societies (Cooperative Credit Societies Act, 1904), but indebtedness remained a serious problem.
The Drain of Wealth theory argued that colonial rule transferred Indian resources to Britain without an equivalent economic return to India.

The theory was developed by Dadabhai Naoroji in 'Poverty and Un-British Rule in India' (1901, based on papers from the 1860s-1870s), and supported by R. C. Dutt ('Economic History of India') and M. G. Ranade. It argued that a part of India's national wealth was transferred to Britain without any economic return.

Components of the drain included 'home charges' (salaries, pensions and leave allowances of British officials, the cost of the India Office in London, interest on public debt, military expenses), profits of British companies, interest on investments in railways (the guaranteed interest system), and payments for British goods and services. Naoroji estimated it at a substantial share of India's national income. The theory became the economic basis of Indian nationalism, showing that British rule impoverished India.
Modern industries such as cotton, jute and other factory sectors developed during colonial rule, though industrial growth took place within a colonial economic structure.

The first cotton mill was started in Bombay in 1854 by C. N. Davar; the cotton textile industry grew in Bombay and Ahmedabad, largely with Indian capital. The jute industry developed around Calcutta from 1855, mostly with British capital. Coal mining (Raniganj), tea plantations (Assam), and later iron and steel, with the Tata Iron and Steel Company (TISCO) founded at Jamshedpur in 1907 by Jamsetji Tata (production began 1912), were important.

Industrial growth was limited by colonial policies: free trade that favoured British goods, lack of tariff protection (until 'discriminating protection' after 1924), the dominance of British managing agency houses, lack of heavy industries and machine-building, and concentration in a few regions. The First and Second World Wars and the Swadeshi movement (1905) gave some boost to Indian industry. Industrial labour grew, and trade unions emerged (AITUC, 1920).

The course traces economic change from the Harappan period to the Guptas. Harappan society combined agriculture with craft production and trade. Early Vedic life gave strong importance to pastoralism, while agriculture became increasingly significant in the Later Vedic period.

The post-Vedic period saw expanding states, towns, crafts and exchange. The Mauryan economy was supported by agriculture, taxation and trade. Gupta economic history includes agrarian change, land grants, trade and coinage.

The long-term picture is therefore one of changing relationships between pastoralism, agriculture, state formation, crafts and commerce.

Harappan economy (c. 2600-1900 BCE): agriculture with wheat, barley and cotton; animal husbandry; specialised crafts (beads, metal, pottery); standardised weights and seals; internal and external trade with Mesopotamia - an advanced urban economy without coins. After its decline, urban life disappeared for over a thousand years.

Vedic economy: the Early Vedic period was pastoral and semi-nomadic, with cattle as wealth and barter exchange; the Later Vedic period saw the use of iron, the clearing of the Ganga valley, settled agriculture (rice, wheat), specialised crafts and the beginning of regular taxes. Post-Vedic (sixth century BCE): the second urbanisation with towns, guilds, punch-marked coins, trade routes and regular revenue collection by the Mahajanapadas.

Mauryan and Gupta economies: the Mauryas had a strong, partly state-controlled economy with land revenue, state monopolies, crown lands, irrigation, roads and trade, as described in the Arthashastra. The post-Mauryan period saw booming crafts, guilds and Indo-Roman trade. The Guptas had an agrarian economy with land grants, gold coinage and continued but changing trade; the feudalism debate concerns this period. Overall, the long-term trend was from pastoralism to settled agriculture, from tribal to state economy, and from barter to money and trade.

The syllabus includes feudalism as a way of examining changes in land and political relations. Long-distance commerce remained important through Indo-Roman and Indian Ocean networks.

Under the Delhi Sultanate, rulers such as Alauddin Khalji and Muhammad bin Tughlaq introduced important economic and fiscal measures. The Mughal economy was strongly agrarian but also supported large towns, craft production and extensive internal and external trade.

Early medieval period: land grants, the growth of landed intermediaries and the decline (or transformation) of trade and towns are discussed through the feudalism debate (Sharma, Kosambi versus Mukhia, Chattopadhyaya). Long-distance trade continued through the Indian Ocean, with Indian, Arab and Southeast Asian merchants; the Indo-Roman trade of the earlier period had brought gold to India. South Indian temples and guilds were important economic institutions.

Delhi Sultanate: Alauddin Khalji's market control (fixed prices, markets, granaries, spies) and revenue reforms (measurement, half of produce, removal of intermediaries' privileges) supported his army. Muhammad bin Tughlaq's experiments (Doab taxation, transfer of capital, token currency, agriculture department) were ambitious but failed. The Sultanate period also saw new technologies (Persian wheel, paper, the spinning wheel), urban growth and trade.

Mughal economy: Akbar's zabt system (Todar Mal), the mansabdari and jagirdari systems, the zamindars, commercial crops, a strong textile industry, large towns, banking (hundis) and extensive trade with Europe and Asia, bringing silver into India. India was one of the world's leading manufacturing economies. Its prosperity also depended on peasants who paid heavy revenue.

sections.title: British Economic Policies and Economic Development

blocks.text:
British rule introduced and expanded land revenue systems that changed rural relationships and placed heavy demands on cultivators in many regions. Rural credit and indebtedness became major economic problems.

Indian nationalist thinkers developed the Drain of Wealth critique to explain the transfer of resources from India to Britain. At the same time, modern industries emerged, including factory-based sectors.

Colonial economic history therefore includes both structural exploitation and important changes in agriculture, finance, trade and industrial production.

Land revenue policies: the Permanent Settlement (1793) created a class of zamindars and fixed revenue; the Ryotwari system made individual cultivators pay directly; the Mahalwari system assessed villages. All imposed heavy demands, encouraged a land market and led to the loss of land by peasants. Commercialisation of agriculture forced peasants to grow cash crops (indigo, cotton, jute, opium) for export. Repeated famines (1770 Bengal, 1876-1878, 1896-1897, 1899-1900, 1943 Bengal) caused millions of deaths.

Rural indebtedness: high revenue in cash, famines and the decline of handicrafts made peasants dependent on moneylenders, who took over land. This led to riots (Deccan, 1875) and laws to protect peasants. Drain of wealth: Naoroji, R. C. Dutt and Ranade argued that home charges, salaries, pensions, profits and interest transferred India's wealth to Britain, causing poverty. Deindustrialisation: the import of British machine-made textiles destroyed traditional handicrafts.

Modern industries: cotton textiles (Bombay, 1854), jute (Calcutta), coal, tea plantations, railways (1853) and iron and steel (TISCO, 1907) developed, but were limited and dominated by British capital, and lacked heavy industry. Indian entrepreneurs (Tata, Birla) grew during the World Wars and the Swadeshi movement. Thus colonial economic history shows both exploitation and certain modernising changes, but the overall effect was underdevelopment and poverty at independence.
